title: Investigative Buddha-Recitation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: In its cultivation there is a graded entry; in its realization there is the truth attained for oneself.

inline.s: (Chan Meditation and Buddha-Recitation Fused into One)
Its cultivation, too, has a graded entry; its realization, too, has the truth attained for oneself.
Use investigation to cut off the faculty of intellect, so that deluded thoughts no longer run on.
In investigation, what counts is courage and diligent vigor; if you do not fiercely press yourself, it cannot be called effort.
The core of investigation: take good care of the mass of doubt
(probing and investigating while without thought)
Probe and investigate before a single thought has sprouted.
Probe and investigate urgently, never letting up day or night.
[Chan Meditation and Buddha-Recitation Fused into One] Master Hanshan said:
"The two practices of Chan and Pure Land were originally not two dharmas; Master Yongming revealed this long ago
(Master Yongming had already taught it in earlier times)
(The Dream Roamings, "Instructions to Shen Dajie")

rows.s: (1) Only the Buddha-Name Remains (Ten Thousand Thoughts Return to One)
(2) Not a Single Thought Arises (the One Returns to Nothing)
(4) Both Subject and Object Extinguished (Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature)

inline.s: Investigative Buddha-recitation (investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?") has its source in the huatou Chan of the Chan school. Ever since Chan Master Dahui of the Southern Song promoted huatou Chan, the practice has centered mainly on investigating the word "wu" (nothing), though there are also many other huatous, for
example the cypress tree in the courtyard, three pounds of flax, a dried shit-stick, the dog has no Buddha-nature, put it down, Mount Sumeru, and so on.

And yet it is already extremely difficult for a Chan practitioner to illuminate the mind and see the nature. Even after illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, one must still do the work of preserving the realization, until the delusions of view and thought are utterly cut off, before one can put an end to birth and death. This is truly difficult beyond difficult. So those who can rely on huatou investigation alone to put an end to birth and death are as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns.

[Delusions of view and thought] Delusions of view and delusions of thought. Delusions of view are the errors of understanding in ordinary beings, such as the five wrong views: the view of a self, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. Delusions of thought are the errors of thinking in ordinary beings, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of sentient beings' drifting through the three realms and suffering birth and death to no purpose; cut them off, and one can put an end to birth and death and escape the three realms.
Thereupon Chan masters of the Ming dynasty such as Chushan Shaoqi, Dufeng Benshan, Tianqi Benrui, and Hanshan Deqing began to advocate investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?"
For example, Master Hanshan instructed:
"To now speak of investigative Buddha-recitation, the intent of which is wondrous awakening
(illuminating the mind and seeing the nature)
, is to take a single utterance of the Buddha as the huatou for investigation
Please note that the huatou of investigative Buddha-recitation is the Buddha-name itself, not "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?"

, which is what is called the public case of reciting the Buddha and investigating Chan. When the ancestral masters of former times taught people to investigate a huatou, it was cases such as the cypress tree in the courtyard, three pounds of flax, a dried shit-stick, the dog has no Buddha-nature, put it down, Mount Sumeru, and the rest. Raise whichever one you like, keep it lodged in your breast, and investigate it silently; by this means cut off the faculty of intellect, so that deluded thoughts no longer run on. When after a long while the huatou gains power, suddenly with a shout of he! it is like a bean bursting in cold ashes; the nest and pit of ignorance and karmic consciousness are shattered at a single blow. This is wondrous awakening. Investigative Buddha-recitation is investigated in just this way: simply raise a single utterance of the Buddha, and immediately examine and question who it is. Probe deeply into whence this Buddha arises, and who ultimately is the one reciting. Doubt on and on like this, investigate again and again, and when after a long while it gains power you will suddenly awaken
(illuminate the mind and see the nature)
. This is the public case of examining the real in Buddha-recitation, and it is no different at all from investigating a huatou."
(The Dream Roamings
A Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)

Because here it is the Buddha-name that serves as the huatou, if a Chan practitioner is fully equipped with faith and vows to be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, then once he succeeds in making the ten thousand thoughts return to one (this is single-mindedness of the Pure Land school), at the end of life he will certainly be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and put an end to birth and death — and moreover he will be born in the upper grades. As for Chan investigation, the return of ten thousand thoughts to one is only a preliminary accomplishment and is easy to attain (in fact, so long as the method is correct and one applies oneself diligently, anyone can reach it; hence Master Yongming said:
"Ten thousand cultivate it, ten thousand go."

). The difficulty of this compared with cutting off the delusions of view and thought is truly the difference between heaven and an abyss. For this reason, investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" became the mainstream of the Chan school after the Ming dynasty.
[And moreover he will be born in the upper grades]
Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing said:

"One who recites thus, with afflictions and the dust of toil neither cut off nor bound, is simply of one mind. Only when one mind is attained may one be called a holder of the name; only then may one be called single-minded and undistracted. When the work of the pure karma is accomplished, one goes straight to the upper grades."
(For details see
An Annotation on A Sure Guide to the West
At this time the Pure Land school also

began to advocate investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" while reciting the Buddha's name, and called it investigative Buddha-recitation, because in this way the mind is easily gathered into one and single-mindedness and undistractedness are attained, and one may further accomplish the Buddha-recitation samādhi.
The advantages of investigative Buddha-recitation are:
investigation holds deluded thoughts at bay, so that the practice becomes a single piece and single-mindedness and undistractedness are reached.
For this reason Master Lianchi (
the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school
) strongly advocated this practice and praised it as a
wondrous dharma
Master Lianchi
said:
"Raising a huatou is the most urgent and vital work for awakening in the school of Chan
(the Chan school)
. A cultivator of the Pure Land
(only one with full faith and vows is a cultivator of the Pure Land)
simply takes a single utterance of the Buddha's name as a huatou
Please note that the huatou of investigative Buddha-recitation is the Buddha-name itself, not "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?"
and this is a wondrous dharma
(The Yunqi Collected Words on the Pure Land)
Moreover, when investigative Buddha-recitation is cultivated to the point where subject and object are both extinguished, one realizes and enters the Buddha-recitation samādhi (for details see
Master Yinguang
Groping for an Elephant: On the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi
[The practice becomes a single piece] When reciting the Buddha's name no deluded thoughts are mixed in — the thought of reciting the Buddha continues unbroken into a single whole piece.
Master Yinguang said:
"If Buddha-recitation cannot be pure and undivided,
one must discipline the mind and not let it gallop outward
, and after a long while it will of itself become pure and undivided. To become a single piece means to be pure and undivided, without admixture."
(The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
A Reply to the Layman Ma Qixi, Letter Four) Master Hanshan said:
"You must take this single utterance of the Buddha
(the Buddha-name)
and bite down hard on it,
resolved to hold out against deluded thoughts

. In every place, let it be present in every thought, and do not be screened and blocked by deluded thoughts. Apply yourself with such bitter and urgent effort, and when after a long while it is pure and familiar, it will of itself respond; without seeking to become a single piece, it will of itself become a single piece."
(The Dream Roamings
Instructions to the Layman Jingxin)

[This is a wondrous dharma] Master Lianchi was one who had passed through investigative Buddha-recitation himself, and half a month beforehand he knew the time of his passing. Master Hanshan's Inscription on the Stupa of Master Lianchi says:
"At first, when the Master
(Master Lianchi)
set out to travel and consult teachers,
he gained power from investigative Buddha-recitation
, and by this he then opened the one gate of the Pure Land, universally gathering the three capacities, and advocated it with all his strength."
(Translation: At first, Master Lianchi traveled on foot to pay respects to good friends in all directions,
gained power from investigative Buddha-recitation

, and at this point opened the one gate of the Pure Land, universally gathering the three capacities of high, middling, and low, and moreover advocated investigative Buddha-recitation with all his strength.) Hence we know that
the one dharma of investigative Buddha-recitation universally gathers the three capacities of high, middling, and low
. The Stupa Inscription also says:
(Master Lianchi)
When death drew near, half a month beforehand he entered the city to take leave of his disciples and old friends."

[The one dharma of investigative Buddha-recitation universally gathers the three capacities of high, middling, and low] In cultivating investigative Buddha-recitation, those of low capacity can accomplish continuous mindfulness of ten recitations at the end of life; those of middling capacity can attain single-mindedness and undistractedness; those of high capacity can realize the Buddha-recitation samādhi (illuminate the mind and see the nature).
Therefore the appearance of investigative Buddha-recitation has two causes:

1. As far as the Chan practitioners of the Chan school are concerned, because here it is the Buddha-name that serves as the huatou, if they are fully equipped with faith and vows to seek birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, then once they succeed in making the ten thousand thoughts return to one (this is single-mindedness of the Pure Land school), at the end of life they will certainly be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and put an end to birth and death. This is far, far easier than cutting off the delusions of view and thought to put an end to birth and death. The Chan school calls this practice "investigating Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" or "the public case of examining the real in Buddha-recitation." In
The Dream Roamings
, "The Essentials of Reciting the Buddha and Investigating Chan"
, Master Hanshan gave detailed instruction on how, through reciting the Buddha's name, to investigate Chan and so
cultivate Chan and Pure Land together (for the annotations
see in full
The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
, "Reciting the Buddha and Investigating Chan"
so that one may both illuminate the mind and see the nature and be assured of putting an end to birth and death in this very life
, escaping the calamity of the three lives

[The calamity of the three lives] Because one cultivates in this life, in the next life one enjoys the reward of blessings; then, leaning on those blessings, one commits evil, and so falls away again in the life after that. Even when the karma of hell is dissolved, one is reborn again as a hungry ghost or an animal, and to regain a human body is difficult beyond difficult! Thus the Buddha asked Ānanda, holding up earth in his hand: "Is there more earth in my hand, or more earth in the great earth?" Ānanda answered, "There is more earth in the great earth." The Buddha said, "Those who gain a human body are like the earth in my hand; those who lose a human body are like the earth of the great earth." Hence "through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, not one person to rely on"! Therefore if a cultivator does not put an end to birth and death in this life, then after three lives suffering and evil retribution are endless — hence the name "the calamity of the three lives." For actual cases of the calamity of the three lives see in full
The Calamity of the Three Lives

2. As far as the Buddha-reciters of the Pure Land school are concerned, if reciting straight through cannot hold deluded thoughts at bay, they therefore use investigation to gather in the mind and hold deluded thoughts at bay. The Pure Land school calls this practice "investigative Buddha-recitation" or "essential-investigation Buddha-recitation." Since investigative Buddha-recitation takes the Buddha-name as its huatou, for a genuine cultivator to reach single-mindedness and undistractedness is by no means beyond reach, and to achieve continuous mindfulness of ten recitations (reciting ten utterances of the Buddha's name without mixing in deluded thoughts) or continuous mindfulness of a hundred recitations (also called a hundred utterances without distraction) is not even worth mentioning. If one makes continuous mindfulness of ten recitations a habit that becomes second nature, so as to achieve continuous mindfulness of ten recitations at the end of life, one will be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth
Therefore investigative Buddha-recitation is a path on which ten thousand cultivate it and ten thousand go.
if reciting straight through cannot hold deluded thoughts at bay

] There are two situations among Buddha-reciters who cultivate diligently: First, reciting straight on, as the days and years increase deluded thoughts grow fewer and fewer, until single-mindedness and undistractedness. Such a person is suited to reciting the Buddha's name straight through.
Second, reciting straight on, as the days and years increase deluded thoughts show no decrease. Such a person is suited to investigative Buddha-recitation.

And so, with the rise of investigative Buddha-recitation, Chan and Pure Land finally merged their streams; Chan meditation and Buddha-recitation were fused into one, and the joint cultivation of Chan and Pure Land spread throughout the world.
In fact, as early as the Tang dynasty, when "Mazu built the monasteries and Baizhang established the pure rules," the Baizhang Pure Rules
("The Essential Principles of the Monastery")
said at the very opening:
"A monastery flourishes when it has no affairs;
cultivation is most secure when it is Buddha-recitation

The second line, "cultivation is most secure when it is Buddha-recitation," means: for the sake of security, a Chan practitioner, while investigating Chan, should also recite the Buddha's name with faith and vows and seek birth in the Pure Land (the joint cultivation of Chan and Pure Land). This is because to be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss through Buddha-recitation and thereby put an end to birth and death, one need only suppress the afflictions; whereas to put an end to birth and death through Chan investigation, one must cut off the afflictions utterly. Compared with the former, the latter is far more difficult, and so the former is the safer road.

[Monastery] A monastery usually refers to a Chan school temple, and so it is also called a Chan grove; but in later ages the temples of the teaching, precepts, and other schools also imitated the Chan grove system and called themselves monasteries. [Mazu built the monasteries] After the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, the Chan school spread throughout the land, but for more than a hundred years masters and disciples only transmitted the Way to one another, mostly dwelling in caves in the rocks or lodging in temples of the Vinaya school. By the Zhenyuan and Yuanhe eras of the Tang dynasty (785-820), the Chan school grew daily more prosperous; its masters often gathered many disciples in one place to cultivate Chan and pursue the Way, yet there were no regulations to govern them. Mazu therefore was the first to build monasteries exclusively for the Chan school, and Baizhang established the pure rules. [Baizhang established the pure rules] Chan Master Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain first established regulations for the Chan groves of the whole land ("The Essential Principles of the Monastery"), later called the Baizhang Pure Rules. [Pure rules] Pure guidelines and procedures. The guidelines they established could purify the assembly, and so they are called pure rules.
Please

take special note: "cultivation is most secure when it is Buddha-recitation" — this was the temple rule first laid down by the ancestral masters of the Chan school when they first built Chan temples! How could it be that Chan and Pure Land cannot stand together? Moreover, in The Records of Pure Land Sages and Saints, those who bore the title of Chan master and were born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss are found everywhere!

In the Song dynasty, Master Yongming, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, who was both a great ancestral master of the Chan school and a great ancestral master of the Pure Land school, advocated the joint cultivation of Chan and Pure Land with all his strength in
the Four Selections:
With Chan but no Pure Land, nine of ten go astray; when the dark realm appears, off you go in a flash.
Without Chan but with Pure Land, ten thousand cultivate and ten thousand go; once you see Amitābha, why worry that you will not awaken
With Chan and with Pure Land, you are like a tiger with horns; in this life a teacher of people, in the next a Buddha or an ancestral master.
Without Chan and without Pure Land, iron beds and bronze pillars await; through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, not one person to rely on.

[Master Yongming, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha] Master Yongming was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, and so his birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, was taken as the sacred birthday of Amitābha Buddha. Of Master Yongming, Master Yinguang praised:
"Master Yongming is a transformation body of Amitābha Buddha. Greatly compassionate and greatly merciful, he opens and transforms sentient beings."
(The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Instructional Dharma Words at the World Buddhist Lay Association)

[Selection] The discriminating and choosing of principles. [Four Selections] Four selections (with Chan but no Pure Land, without Chan but with Pure Land, with Chan and with Pure Land, and without Chan and without Pure Land). For the annotations to the Four Selections see in full
The Joint Cultivation of Chan and Pure Land

. [With Chan] Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature (seeing the original nature through and through). [With Pure Land] True faith and earnest vows, reciting the Buddha's name to single-mindedness and undistractedness. [Without Chan] Not having illuminated the mind and seen the nature. [Without Pure Land] Not having achieved "true faith and earnest vows, reciting the Buddha's name to single-mindedness and undistractedness." [Why worry that you will not awaken] Why worry that you will not illuminate the mind and see the nature.
"With Chan and with Pure Land, you are like a tiger with horns; in this life a teacher of people, in the next a Buddha or an ancestral master"

: one who has both illuminated the mind and seen the nature and has true faith and earnest vows, reciting the Buddha's name to single-mindedness and undistractedness, is like a tiger with horns, matchless in majesty and power. In this life he is a teacher of the multitude, and at the end of life he is born in the highest grade of the upper birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, becoming a Buddha in one lifetime.
[Like a tiger with horns] Master Yinguang said:
"One who is like a tiger with horns, because such a person cultivates Chan and Pure Land together
, has great wisdom, great samādhi, and great eloquence
. Demons and outsiders lose their courage at the mention of his name, like a tiger with horns, majestic and without peer."
(The
Dharma Words of the Shanghai Dharma Assembly for Averting Disaster and Protecting the Nation

) In this passage of instruction one can fully see Master Yinguang's affirmation of and praise for the joint cultivation of Chan and Pure Land. [Without peer (chou)] There is no one who can compare with him.

In the Ming dynasty, moreover, Master Hanshan set us a shining example of the joint cultivation of Chan and Pure Land. Not only did he attain the highest accomplishment in actual practice and in doctrine, but he himself cultivated investigative Buddha-recitation; not only was he born in the Pure Land at ease, but he realized the indestructible diamond body (for details see
The Life of Master Hanshan
). He also gave concrete instruction on how, through reciting the Buddha's name, to investigate Chan (for details see
The Dream Roamings
, "The Essentials of Reciting the Buddha and Investigating Chan"
and
and
advocated with all his strength that
all Dharma gates should point toward the Pure Land
. In
The Dream Roamings
, "Preface to Pointing Toward the Pure Land"
, the Master instructed:
If the one gate of the Pure Land
covers all three capacities alike, so that the sudden and the gradual enter together, and no faculty is left ungathered — what is called crossing the three realms horizontally —
then it is the most supreme Dharma gate
. Among the ancestral masters of former times, among those who awakened the mind,
there was not one who did not take this as his final home
, such as Nagarjuna
(Bodhisattva Nagarjuna)
and Ashvaghosha
(Bodhisattva Ashvaghosha)
, who praised it with all their strength."
He also said:
Among those of the highest capacity in the Chan school, there is not one who does not return to the Pure Land.
(For details see
Master Hanshan's Buddha-Recitation and Rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
[He himself (Master Hanshan) cultivated investigative Buddha-recitation] Master Hanshan records in his Chronological Biography:
"In the forty-fourth year of the Jiajing era
, the year yichou, I
was twenty years old.
In the tenth month of that winter, Master Yungu established a Chan session at Tianjie
(Tianjie Temple)
, gathering fifty-three of the famous and virtuous men of the land
(he gathered fifty-three men of repute and virtue from within the country)
, and opened the Dharma gate of seated meditation. The Master urged me strongly to go and join them, and at that time the junior master Weng consented
(at that time the abbot of Baoen Temple, where Master Hanshan was, the junior ancestral master, agreed that he might go)
, and so I was able to join the assembly
(take part in the gathering)
. At first I did not know the secret of applying the mind, and suffered greatly. So I offered incense and asked for instruction
(so I burned incense and bowed to ask for teaching)
, and the Master instructed me in the public case of examining the real in Buddha-recitation
(investigative Buddha-recitation)
From then on I investigated, not moving a single thought
. Within three months I was as if in a dream, never seeing the great assembly at all, nor knowing that there were any daily affairs."
(For details see
Annotated Commentary on the Chronological Biography of Master Hanshan

What is more, the Avatamsaka Sutra is the supremely comprehensive teaching spoken by our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha out of his own nature after his enlightenment; it has long borne the name of king of sutras,
and its conclusion has Bodhisattva Samantabhadra's ten great kingly vows leading back to the Pure Land
(for details see the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Conduct and Vows).

Yet, to our regret, through the ages biased people within the two schools of Chan and Pure Land have recklessly set up sectarian views. Those Chan followers who did not understand Pure Land cultivation wantonly opposed and slandered the Pure Land school, and who knows how many Chan practitioners (including themselves) they misled so that they could not escape the six paths of rebirth. And those Pure Land followers who did not understand Chan cultivation wantonly opposed and slandered the Chan school, advocating distracted Buddha-recitation and the certainty of rebirth through merely calling the name, and who knows how many Buddha-reciters (including themselves) they misled so that they could not escape the six paths of rebirth. They all believed they were spreading the Dharma and saving beings, when in fact they were slandering the Dharma, harming both others and themselves.
Cause and effect are plain to see, and retribution never fails; this is truly a tragedy of the greatest magnitude!
Q: It is said that Master Yinguang was opposed to investigative Buddha-recitation. Why then do you teach it?
A: When the ancestral masters guide students they prescribe medicine according to the illness.

For example, The Dream Roamings records that Master Hanshan taught some students to contemplate the mind, others to investigate Chan, others to recite the Buddha's name, and others to recite mantras — all according to the particular circumstances of those people. Therefore one instruction cannot be used to negate another, and still less can instructions given according to particular circumstances be presented as what the ancestral master said to everyone.
Master Yinguang was not opposing investigative Buddha-recitation; he was cautioning those who have no foundation, or who do not attend to faith and vows.

[Having no foundation] Having no foundation is not something fixed and unchangeable. If you know that you have no foundation, then follow the chapter on "Preliminary Practice" in this article and build the foundation up, and you will have one. In cultivation, examples of those who come from behind and rise to preeminence are too numerous to count. The key is to apply effort, and to know how to apply it.

And as for the Pure Land students who already have a foundation and are fully equipped with faith and vows, Master Yinguang explained in detail in Groping for an Elephant: On the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi how to practice investigative Buddha-recitation. For example:
One must, upon this
(same as "this")
single thought of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha,'
examine it again and again
, and keep it vividly in mind without letting go."
And he explained in detail the states and benefits of realizing the fruit through investigative Buddha-recitation:

"As for its benefits: in the present, though not yet apart from the Sahā world, one constantly joins the assembly in the ocean of lotuses; at the end of life, one immediately ascends to the upper grades and instantly realizes the Buddha vehicle."

(Translation: As for the benefits of realizing the Buddha-recitation samādhi: though in the present one has not yet left the Sahā world, one constantly joins the lotus-pool ocean assembly of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. When death draws near, one immediately ascends to the upper grades and is born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and upon arriving there instantly realizes the Buddha vehicle.)

Master Yinguang (the thirteenth patriarch of the Pure Land school) worried that speaking of investigative Buddha-recitation in Groping for an Elephant: On the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi would provoke the quarrel "Is this Chan? Is this Pure Land?" So in that text he especially warned, with words that came from the bottom of his heart:
Do not speak of it to outsiders.
For only when one's state has reached that step does one know its perfect fusion and ultimate completeness. Master Yinguang said:
"Only one of the family knows the affairs of the family; tell it to an outsider, and slander is certain beyond doubt."
(For details see
Master Yinguang
Groping for an Elephant: On the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi
[Tell it to an outsider, and slander is certain beyond doubt] Although Master Yongming, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, long ago instructed:
"With Chan and with Pure Land, you are like a tiger with horns; in this life a teacher of people, in the next a Buddha or an ancestral master."
still many people of the Pure Land school turn pale at the mention of Chan. Prejudice runs deep and has lasted long; even Master Yinguang sighed and said:
"Slander is certain beyond doubt!"
In fact, whether something is a Pure Land practice depends on whether faith and vows are complete. Master Ouyi (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
"If a Chan practitioner wishes to be born in the West, he need not change to Buddha-recitation; let him but be equipped with faith and vows, and Chan investigation is itself a Pure Land practice."
(Master Ouyi's Pure Land Collection
Casual Talks from the Brahma Chamber)
What is more, the condition for rebirth is continuous mindfulness of ten recitations at the end of life (for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth

). For Buddha-reciters fully equipped with faith and vows, whichever way makes it easy to keep mindfulness continuous, and even to reach single-mindedness and undistractedness, is the way they should recite; this is only natural, and there is nothing objectionable in it. Whether to recite straight on or to practice investigative Buddha-recitation should be chosen by each person according to his own circumstances.

The author often thinks of how many Buddha-reciters have recited for a dozen years or even several decades without achieving so much as a hundred utterances without distraction, and he sighs and wrings his hands endlessly. This has nothing to do with capacity; it is entirely because they have not found a method of Buddha-recitation suited to themselves! Hence the ancients said:
"In cultivation there is nothing else to cultivate; you need only know the road's head
(it is only a matter of finding a method of cultivation suited to yourself)
; once the road's head is known
(once you have found a method of cultivation suited to yourself)
, birth and death come to rest together."

[A hundred utterances without distraction] Within one hundred utterances of the Buddha's name, to keep the Buddha-name clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered (without deluded thoughts). [Entirely because they have not found a method of Buddha-recitation suited to themselves] I have heard of an old woman who, when reciting the Buddha's name, could not stop her deluded thoughts; in a fury she banged her head against the wall, saying as she banged, 'Take that, deluded thoughts! Take that, deluded thoughts!' People asked her, 'What happened after you banged?' She said, 'Still deluded thoughts!' A Buddha-reicter with such determination as this, if she found a method of Buddha-recitation suited to herself and cultivated it steadily and practically, would attain not only a hundred utterances without distraction but even single-mindedness and undistractedness. But if one has not found a method of Buddha-recitation that stops deluded thoughts, banging one's head against the wall is of no use either.
Master Lianchi (
the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school
) instructed:
"Dufeng and Tianqi both taught investigative Buddha-recitation; why did Konggu say
there is no need to use such a method
It is because the capacities they met with were different
this was said with regard to different capacities
, and so each may follow his own convenience without hindrance
(each person may do as he pleases — each chooses according to his own actual circumstances, and that is right)
(Encouragement at the Chan Gate)
[It is because the capacities they met with were different]

For some people investigation suits their capacity and brings real results, and they may use investigative Buddha-recitation; for others reciting straight through suits their capacity and brings real results, and they need only recite straight on.
Master Lianchi
also said:
"In our dynasty
(meaning the present dynasty)
during the Hongwu and Yongle eras
(the years of Hongwu and Yongle)

, there were the three great elders Konggu, Tianqi, and Dufeng. In their discussions of Buddha-recitation, Masters Tian and Du both taught people to look into 'Who is reciting the Buddha's name?'; only Konggu said that 'merely reciting straight through also has a gate of awakening.' These two
(reciting straight through and investigating)
each follow what suits the capacity, and both are right
(both are correct)
. And Konggu merely said that reciting straight through is also acceptable
(moreover, Master Konggu only said that reciting straight through is also acceptable)
he did not say that investigation is wrong
(he did not say that investigation is mistaken)
The Second Bamboo Window Collection
Master Ouyi's Treatise on Investigative Buddha-Recitation says:
"Q: If the Pure Land is primary, can investigation serve as Buddha-recitation? A: Investigation
(investigation)
and recitation
(reciting straight through)
both fall under practice; if one is earnest, investigation too brings rebirth
(if one is diligent, investigation also brings rebirth)
, and if one is not earnest, recitation too brings no rebirth
(if one is not diligent, reciting straight through also cannot bring rebirth)
. Further, though one's practice be earnest
(though one's practice be diligent)
, if faith and vows guide it, one is reborn; if faith and vows do not guide it, one is not reborn."

This means: for a cultivator of the Pure Land, reciting straight through can bring rebirth, and investigation can also bring rebirth; the key is to be diligent and to be fully equipped with faith and vows.

Therefore, if you find that reciting straight through works well for you, then recite straight through, and there is no need to slander investigative Buddha-recitation; if you find that investigative Buddha-recitation works well for you, then practice investigative Buddha-recitation, and there is no need to slander reciting straight through. For everyone's circumstances are different!
Q: It is said that investigative Buddha-recitation
suits only people of good capacity. Is that so?
A: This is because
for several hundred years many have practiced investigative Buddha-recitation, few have persevered, and fewer still have finally succeeded; and so a view has formed:
investigative Buddha-recitation
suits only people of good capacity.
In fact, this view is wrong.
The reasons why "

many have practiced investigative Buddha-recitation, few have persevered, and fewer still have finally succeeded" are two: first, people plunged into investigation without first laying a foundation, so that only those of good capacity could get a handle on it and persevere; second,
the road was unclear, and they had to grope their way forward entirely on their own.

As a result only those of good capacity could find a truly effective road and so succeed. And those who practiced blindly and recklessly were everywhere, with nothing to show for it. In this way the illusion arose that "investigative Buddha-recitation suits only people of good capacity."

[Those who practiced blindly and recklessly were everywhere] To say nothing of ordinary Chan practitioners and Buddha-reciters, just look at those through the ages who have led assemblies and given instructions: most of them took "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" as the huatou, and still less did they investigate apart from mind and consciousness.
The fact is this:
so long as
"the foundation is well laid, the method of investigation is correct, the cultivation is diligent, and faith and vows are complete"
, investigative Buddha-recitation
can be practiced by anyone, and anyone can thereby put an end to birth and death: ten thousand cultivate it, ten thousand go.
Q: Are essential-investigation Buddha-recitation and investigative Buddha-recitation one or two?

A: The two are one; essential-investigation Buddha-recitation is another name for investigative Buddha-recitation. In his instructions Master Lianchi used both the word "investigation" and the word "essential investigation." For example:
In The Yunqi Collected Dharma Words, Master Lianchi says:
"To now 'investigate
the act of investigation
', this is still one gate, not two matters. If
investigation
is not convenient, then reciting straight through will also do."
He also said:
"Q: Chan investigation prizes the non-arising of a single thought; Buddha-recitation prizes the continuation of pure mindfulness. This one gate, namely
investigative Buddha-recitation
, has as its intent wondrous awakening together with rebirth."
He also said:

Truly, if one can see through this very thought of reciting the Buddha's name at its arising, one may be sure the great matter is finished. Yet one must not, on seeing such words, set to work to think and conjecture, to force an interpretation and seek to comprehend, for then one loses it instead. Simply investigate
essentially
in every thought, truly accumulating effort over time until you attain it yourself — that is realization-awakening.

(Translation: Truly speaking, if one can see through this very thought of reciting the Buddha's name at its arising, one may be sure the great matter of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is finished. Yet one must not, on seeing me say 'if one can see through this very thought of reciting the Buddha's name at its arising, one may be sure the great matter is finished,' set to work to think and conjecture about the meaning of these words, forcing an interpretation in order to comprehend them. If one does so, one loses the true purport instead. Simply apply yourself single-mindedly in the state without thought to realize and examine it; thus truly applying effort and accumulating power, one will attain it oneself in time — only this is realization-awakening.)
[Think and conjecture (
bu
) and measure] To think and conjecture. [Force an interpretation and seek to comprehend] To force a strained interpretation in order to comprehend.
He also said:
Essential investigation

means: hearing the Buddha's name, one not only recollects it but turns the thought back to observe it, examines it to the ultimate, and interrogates its source. When essential investigation reaches its limit, one suddenly fuses with one's own original mind."
[Interrogates its source] To investigate its source to the very bottom. "Interrogate (ju)," read "ju," means to investigate exhaustively; "source" means the original face (the original nature).
He also said:

"Suffering arises from the body, the body arises from karma, and so on. Illness is one among sufferings, and its causing one another in turn is likewise so. One should diligently and minutely, day and night,
investigate essentially

. If investigation does not succeed, one need only raise the huatou of one's own fundamental investigation, the Buddha-recitation, and turn the light to look within. When you know the settling place of this thought, delusion breaks of itself. When delusion breaks, it is worn away in turn, and likewise so."

(Translation: Suffering arises from the body, the body arises from karma, and karma arises from delusion. Illness is one among sufferings, and so delusion, karma, body, and suffering also cause one another in turn. One should diligently (with unremitting care) and minutely (with fine attention), day and night, investigate essentially. If investigation does not succeed, one need only raise the huatou of one's own fundamental investigation, the Buddha-recitation (the Buddha-name), and probe within: Who is reciting the Buddha's name? When you know the settling place of this thought, delusion breaks of itself. When delusion breaks, karma breaks; when karma breaks, the body breaks; when the body breaks, suffering (illness) breaks; and so it is worn away in turn.)
In the Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitābha Sutra, Master Lianchi says:
"It is not known that
essential-investigation Buddha-recitation

is extremely similar in intent to the former venerable masters' teaching people to raise a huatou and give rise to doubt. Therefore it is said that in Chan investigation there is no need to raise any other huatou; one need only settle upon a single utterance of Amitābha Buddha. How wondrous are these words!"
In The Second Bamboo Window Collection, Master Lianchi devoted a whole chapter to "
Investigative Buddha-Recitation
," saying:
In our dynasty
the present dynasty
during the Hongwu and Yongle eras
the years of Hongwu and Yongle

, there were the three great elders Konggu, Tianqi, and Dufeng. In their discussions of Buddha-recitation, Masters Tian and Du both taught people to look into "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?"; only Konggu said that merely reciting straight through also has a gate of awakening.
Q: Why did Master Ouyi say in his Treatise on Investigative Buddha-Recitation that investigative Buddha-recitation "has great benefit, and also great harm"?
A:
Master Shandao and other ancestral masters all instructed
continuity itself is rebirth
(for details see
Continuity Itself Is Rebirth
And yet

in present-day society, with information flooding everywhere, material desires running rampant, and people's minds in turmoil, those of superior capacity who can hold deluded thoughts at bay by reciting straight through and so achieve continuous mindfulness are no longer many. Investigative Buddha-recitation, however, uses investigation to cut off the faculty of intellect and stop deluded thoughts from running on, and thus achieves continuous mindfulness.
It is truly a wondrous dharma suited to the present time
. — This is the great benefit of investigative Buddha-recitation.
As for
the great harm of investigative Buddha-recitation, Master Ouyi instructed:

"As for the great harm: once one becomes involved in investigation, one relies solely on one's own spirit and does not seek the power of the Buddha, wishing only to bring it forth in this present life
(to be resolved to illuminate the mind and see the nature in this very life)
, and no longer vows to be born
(and no longer seeks birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)

. Or, doubt giving rise to obstruction, one says that one cannot be born; in extreme cases one sets aside the ten thousand practices and abandons the scriptures. The ancients' original intent was to gather Chan back into the Pure Land and to open this provisional device within the Chan school; people today misunderstand it, and many go so far as to abandon the Pure Land and follow Chan, so that within the Pure Land school it turns into a destruction of the Dharma. Wholly departing from the true cause of pure karma, how can one hope to be born in that land?"

This was Master Ouyi's instruction given under the circumstances of his time, when the Chan school was flourishing, out of concern that some might abandon the Pure Land and follow Chan because of investigative Buddha-recitation.

But as far as present actual circumstances are concerned, even the most basic single-mindedness and undistractedness is spoken of as something mysterious and beyond reach; and how many people are there who in this life would cut off all afflictions and put an end to birth and death by their own power, abandoning the Pure Land and following Chan? So investigative Buddha-recitation today no longer has the great harm of "abandoning the Pure Land and following Chan" that Master Ouyi spoke of in his day;
only the great benefit remains

. Moreover, in today's situation, where false and perverse teachings such as "distracted Buddha-recitation" and "rebirth is certain through merely calling the name" run wild, the great benefit of investigative Buddha-recitation shines all the more brightly.
If a student of Buddhism does not practice investigative Buddha-recitation, it is to enter a mountain of treasures and return empty-handed.
[Today's false and perverse teachings
such as "distracted Buddha-recitation" and "rebirth is certain through merely calling the name"

running wild] There are two kinds of people who advocate "distracted Buddha-recitation" and "rebirth is certain through merely calling the name." One kind has taken wrong views into their minds and cannot extricate themselves; the other kind, because reciting straight through over the long term has not brought them continuous mindfulness and single-minded Buddha-recitation, follows these false teachings, waving banners and shouting, to console and reassure themselves (though in truth their minds are not at peace). If people of this latter kind would practice investigative Buddha-recitation steadily and practically, they would certainly achieve continuous mindfulness and single-minded Buddha-recitation, and then they would no longer believe in "distracted Buddha-recitation" and "rebirth is certain through merely calling the name." This too is one of the great benefits of investigative Buddha-recitation.
Q: Master Ouyi instructed:
"Or, doubt giving rise to obstruction, one says that one cannot be born; in extreme cases one sets aside the ten thousand practices and abandons the scriptures."
Is this not a great harm of investigative Buddha-recitation?
A:

"Doubt giving rise to obstruction" refers to investigating with the mind and consciousness, taking deluded thoughts for the mass of doubt. So the harm of "doubt giving rise to obstruction" is not caused by cultivating investigative Buddha-recitation at all, but by not understanding how to cultivate it; how can the two be lumped together? For details see
Investigating Apart from Mind and Consciousness
Q: Why is there no investigative Buddha-recitation in the book Essentials of Buddha-Recitation?

A: The book Essentials of Buddha-Recitation is very good, but it is most regrettable that in compiling the Dharma words of the ancestral masters it took the position that "investigation is unnecessary" (for details see the editorial note to "Volume One: A Guide to Buddha-Recitation"), and excluded the instructions concerning investigative Buddha-recitation. This is where the book falls short of perfection: it failed to appreciate the painstaking care with which ancestral masters such as Hanshan and Lianchi promoted investigative Buddha-recitation within the Pure Land school, and so lost the essence of the methods of Buddha-recitation (as stated above, Master Lianchi called investigative Buddha-recitation
"a wondrous dharma."
). I hope someone will supply what is missing, to complete the whole.
the painstaking care with which they promoted investigative Buddha-recitation within the Pure Land school
] By the late Ming, people's minds had sunk ever lower, and those who could hold afflictions at bay by reciting straight through grew fewer; therefore
ancestral masters such as Hanshan and Lianchi
prescribed medicine according to the illness

, and promoted investigative Buddha-recitation within the Pure Land school. How could one say that "investigation is unnecessary"? That truly betrays the ancestral masters' painstaking care, and has left this
wondrous dharma suited to the times
sunk in oblivion to this day.

The minds of sentient beings are scattered, like wild horses and cunning monkeys, galloping and leaping wildly without a moment's rest. To begin investigating in the midst of such a thicket of deluded thoughts is to find it hard to get a handle on, or hard to sustain, and it may even cause physical discomfort. This is the main reason many people give up after investigating for a while. Therefore, before practicing investigative Buddha-recitation, it is best first to cultivate the preliminary practice and lay a foundation. The firmer the foundation, the smoother and more effective all later cultivation will be.
There are many methods for laying the foundation; for example, the book
The Chan of Awareness

introduces many kinds of methods. The method for laying the foundation in this article is to be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, in order to cultivate an awareness that is focused, continuous, and lasting, and so lay a solid foundation for investigative Buddha-recitation.

There are mainly two ways of breathing: thoracic breathing and abdominal breathing. Thoracic breathing relies chiefly on the movement of the ribs and breastbone; when inhaling, the chest expands front to back and side to side. Because during breathing the air goes directly into the lungs, the chest cavity expands accordingly while the abdomen stays flat. The breathing in this article uses the natural abdominal method of abdominal breathing: that is, when inhaling the abdominal muscles expand (the abdomen rises), and when exhaling the abdominal muscles contract (the abdomen falls). Compared with thoracic breathing, this method of breathing has many benefits for physical health. (For details see
Abdominal Breathing

When you inhale, the abdomen gradually rises; at that time be single-mindedly aware of the process of the abdomen rising, and note "rising" in the mind. When you exhale, the abdomen gradually falls; at that time be single-mindedly aware of the process of the abdomen falling, and note "falling" in the mind. The essential point is this: keep up continuous awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen. When first practicing, you may place a hand on the abdomen to feel its rising and falling.
Breathe naturally, and simply be single-mindedly aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, placing your attention on the rising and falling of the abdomen.

So long as you are aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, there will be no deluded thoughts. If a deluded thought arises, it means you have lost awareness; you must at once draw your attention back and be single-mindedly aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen. Lost it, draw it back; lost it, draw it back; ...... If you spend a whole hour in this tug-of-war, not one minute of that hour has been wasted. As you keep practicing you will find that you lose awareness fewer and fewer times, and that the interval between losing it and drawing it back grows shorter and shorter. This is progress.

When you are relatively sure of your awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen, go a step further and become aware of the sensations in the process of the abdomen rising and falling (and do not pay attention to the outer shape of the abdomen).

While aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, if deluded thoughts blaze up and are rather hard to draw back, then do not force yourself to draw them back; instead, single-mindedly observe the deluded thoughts, see what they want to think about, and label and classify them: "scattered," "random thinking," "planning," and so on. When the deluded thoughts have weakened, return to being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen.

In Chan cultivation there are only these two things: being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen and observing deluded thoughts, and of the two, being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen is primary; the two are applied in flexible alternation.

Outside the times of dedicated practice, you should practice whenever you can find a spare moment, and try to maintain awareness of each movement in your daily activities (you may consult the chapter "Awareness of Movement" in
The Chan of Awareness

). In short, seize every opportunity to practice awareness and cultivate the power of awareness; this is the basic skill of investigative Buddha-recitation. Never make light of any one- or two-minute opportunity to practice!

At the beginning, practice mainly in the sitting and lying positions. Then gradually come to practice while walking and while standing as well. (When walking in meditation, you may take four steps to one inhalation and four steps to one exhalation.) In this way, throughout the twelve periods of the day, walking, standing, sitting, and lying are all spent doing the work; your skill will improve quickly and your adaptability will be strong.
When you lie down to sleep, you should also be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, right up to the last moment before falling asleep.

When your awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen is clear and single-pointed, you may enter investigative Buddha-recitation. And even during the stage of investigative Buddha-recitation, do not forget to take time regularly to be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, so as to deepen and consolidate the basic skill. The firmer the basic skill, the smoother and more effective the investigation.
Here is a practice greatly beneficial to body and mind, one that cultivates both nature and life:
thought-free deep breathing.
The method is this: each breath lasts

seconds (you may practice facing a clock with a second hand); the time of exhalation equals or is slightly longer than the time of inhalation, and you may also hold the breath for two or three seconds at the turn between inhalation and exhalation. During the breathing you must clearly be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, and thus be without thought. Do it twice a day for
minutes each time, and also do it whenever and wherever you can find a spare moment.
Q: Is noting the same as silently reciting in the mind?

A: No. If you silently recite "rising" and "falling" along with the rising and falling of the abdomen, then once the recitation becomes familiar this will happen: in fact you have already forgotten to be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, yet the mind is still mechanically reciting "rising" and "falling." Noting, however, is this: when you are aware of the abdomen rising, you tell yourself that this is "rising"; when you are aware of the abdomen falling, you tell yourself that this is "falling." If there is no awareness, there is no noting.
Q: What sitting posture should be used in Chan cultivation?

A: Chan cultivation runs through walking, standing, sitting, and lying. A disciple of the Buddha should have dignified bearing: outwardly dignified in bearing, inwardly upright in mind. When standing, have the manner of standing; when sitting, have the manner of sitting. When sitting in meditation, choose a posture in which you can sit for a long time. You may sit cross-legged, or sit upright on a chair or stool (with the back away from the backrest, so that the energy channels flow freely), with both legs hanging down. Once seated, keep the back and head straight (this is very important), but not rigid.
1. Only the Buddha-Name Remains (Ten Thousand Thoughts Return to One)
2. Not a Single Thought Arises (the One Returns to Nothing)
3. Concentration and Wisdom Equally Held
4. Both Subject and Object Extinguished (Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature)
The method of investigative Buddha-recitation is this:

raise a single utterance of the Buddha-name (Amitābha Buddha), and immediately gather your spirit and probe within: Who is reciting the Buddha's name? When after a long while a deluded thought arises, raise another utterance of the Buddha-name, and again thus gather your spirit and probe within: Who is reciting the Buddha's name? If no deluded thought arises, then simply keep probing.
So long as you are probing in focused and continuous fashion, no deluded thought will arise

; if a deluded thought does arise, it means your spirit has scattered, your probing has slackened, or you have even gone astray. At that time you must immediately raise a single utterance of the Buddha-name, again gather your spirit and turn the light around to shine within, and probe in focused and continuous fashion: Who is reciting the Buddha's name
Deluded thoughts arise in the gaps of probing, and blaze up when probing is lost.

[Deluded thoughts arise in the gaps of probing] For a beginner, probing is not continuous, even though he believes he is probing with concentrated attention. Therefore, in the early stage of investigative Buddha-recitation, the task is to make the probing continuous, even if only for a brief time. So long as you investigate persistently according to the method described above, brief stretches of continuity will of themselves appear. During those brief stretches you are in the state without thought, with nothing but probing; this is usually called the arising of the mass of doubt. As days pass and the work deepens, these brief moments of the mass of doubt will join into stretches, and even into a single piece.

Once the work of investigation gets going, in fact you begin probing within at the very moment you recite the Buddha's name. There may be intervals between one utterance of the Buddha-name and the next, but the probing should have no intervals at all; it must be unbroken.

What is called investigation is probing within. In investigative Buddha-recitation the Buddha-name is the huatou, and one investigates: "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" The method of investigation is: probe into who is reciting the Buddha's name. Use probing to cut off the faculty of intellect, so that deluded thoughts no longer run on.
The state in which one is probing and without thought is the mass of doubt.

Investigation means taking good care of the mass of doubt, so that it becomes a stretch, then a single piece, then a single mass (enveloping the whole body). The work of investigation must not be separated from one's walking or standing, and must not be neglected day or night; it makes no distinction between movement and stillness, and in every thought it is unbroken.
Master Hanshan said:
"Investigative Buddha-recitation is investigated in just this way. Simply raise a single utterance of the Buddha, and immediately examine and question who it is; probe deeply
and investigate
, whence this Buddha
arises
(whence this Buddha-name arises)
, and who ultimately is the one reciting
(who ultimately is the one reciting the Buddha's name)
? Doubt on and on like this, investigate again and again, and when after a long while it gains power you will suddenly awaken
(illuminate the mind and see the nature)
(The Dream Roamings
A Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)
[Not separated from one's walking or standing
, and not neglected day or night
] Do the work in this way, and you will make the mass of doubt into a single piece. Chan Master Gaofeng said:
"Through the twelve periods
the twenty-four hours)
of the day, let there be no interval. Rise at the fourth watch and at once feel for the huatou
(for this article, this means giving rise to the mass of doubt — probing while without thought)

, and set it before you. If you feel at all drowsy, then get up and set foot on the ground, and that too is the huatou. When walking, do not be apart from the huatou at any step. When opening your bundle and spreading your bowl, when picking up the spoon and setting down the chopsticks, in all the affairs you share with the assembly, never be apart from the huatou. Day and night, likewise so. There has never been one who made it into a single piece and did not awaken
(become enlightened)
Encouragement at the Chan Gate)
Master Hanshan instructed:

"If you can truly apply the mind, then work solely at the point before a single thought arises. When after a long while it is pure and familiar, not a single thought arises and the original substance appears before you. The eternal light shines bright and clear; it does not change with darkness or light, and movement and stillness are one suchness. Only then is it called making it into a single piece."
(The Dream Roamings
A Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)

[Making no distinction between movement and stillness, in every thought unbroken] Whether in movement or in stillness, one probes within without a break in any thought. On this point, Elder Master Xuyun instructed:

As for what is called movement and stillness, the beginner must not fail to examine it. Walking, standing, being in the hall, doing tasks, greeting and seeing off, talking and laughing, urinating and defecating — these are called movement; sitting and lying quietly at ease are called stillness. Examine it minutely like this
(examine it minutely in this way)
: throughout the twelve periods of the day
(throughout the twenty-four hours)
, at what times am I in movement and yet not carried away by movement
(still probing within)
? At what times am I in stillness and yet not turned by stillness
(still probing within)
? In the face of all conditions, does the mind arise or not? If one can examine in this way
(if one can truly examine in this way)
, then in movement one is not carried away by movement
(in movement no deluded thoughts arise)
, and one can be awake and yet still
(that is, awake and yet still)
; in stillness one is not turned by stillness
(in stillness one does not fall into dullness)
, and that is still and yet awake
(that is, still and yet awake)
The Chan Dharma of Xuyun
[Still and yet awake]
It means: without thought and yet not losing the awareness that illuminates.
Still
means not a single thought arises;
awake

means the spirit is clear and does not lose the awareness that illuminates (for this article, does not lose the probing). Master Yongjia said: "Still and awake is right; still and blank is wrong. Awake and still is right; awake and full of thoughts is wrong."
[Blank] Here it means muddled (having lost the awareness that illuminates).

The essential point is this: gather your spirit and turn the light around to shine within; with focus, continuity, and persistence, probe into who is reciting the Buddha's name, so as to deepen the mass of doubt and take good care of it — as the saying goes, "Great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening."

In the course of investigation, awakening comes from doubt (the mass of doubt), and doubt comes from faith. It is of utmost importance that one's faith be sincere and firm, and that one investigate without yielding, overcoming every difficulty.
Chan Master Gaofeng said:
"You should know that doubt
(the mass of doubt)

takes faith as its substance, and awakening takes doubt as its function. If faith is ten parts, doubt is ten parts; if doubt reaches ten parts, awakening reaches ten parts — as when the water rises, the boat floats higher."
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gaofeng Yuanmiao)
The ancients said:
"Raise a mass of doubt through your whole body."
Please savor this famous saying well!
Probing within is fusing with the self-nature.

When you probe within, focused and without deluded thoughts, body and mind will have a wondrous feeling; this is the feeling of the original substance (the self-nature, that master who recites the Buddha's name), and it is an entry into the original substance (a fusing with the self-nature)
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Not apart from the self-nature — that is the field of blessing."
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch)

[Not apart from the self-nature — that is the field of blessing] When one fuses with the self-nature, one no longer deludedly clings to the body and mind of the five aggregates as self; instead the master within is in charge, still and yet knowing. This is planting the greatest field of blessing.
Master Hanshan said:
"Therefore the Buddhadharma teaches people to take
(to take solely)
the cutting off of deluded thoughts as the foundation,
(because)

deluded thoughts are the root of all evil karma of greed, hatred, and delusion. Even a bodhisattva's cultivation up to Buddhahood, and the reward of the most supreme, majestic, vast, and great field of blessing in the heavens and among humans, all begin with cutting off deluded thoughts. For when
(since)
deluded thoughts are cut off, evil karma dissolves; when evil karma dissolves, a hundred blessings gather — this is what is called seeking abundant blessing for oneself
(this is seeking abundant blessing for oneself)
(The Dream Roamings
Instructions to Zhong Hengying)
Fusing with the self-nature:
the self-nature is the inner spiritual power, that master within the body
, that master who recites the Buddha's name

. To fuse with the self-nature is to feel it, to become one with it, and to abide in it. For sentient beings, the body is the dwelling of the self-nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
"The physical body is a lodging house."
Patriarch Linji said:
"Just see the puppets played on the stage; all their pulling and tugging comes from the man inside."
This means that the physical body is like a wooden puppet, and it is the self-nature that gives the physical body its life. Hence the Formula for Cultivating the Mind says:
"The hundred bones
(the physical body)
collapse and scatter, returning to fire and wind
(the four elements separate)
; one thing
(the self-nature)
is forever
(eternally)
numinous, covering heaven and earth."

Throughout the twelve hours of the day and night, knowing hunger and knowing thirst, knowing cold and knowing heat, sometimes angry and sometimes glad — this is the self-nature. The physical body is a gathering of the four conditions earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is inert and insentient — how could it see, hear, feel, and know? That which can see, hear, feel, and know must be your own self-nature. The patriarch says:

"The four great elements do not understand how to expound the Dharma or listen to the Dharma; space does not understand how to expound the Dharma or listen to the Dharma. Only that which is vivid and clearly alone before your eyes, without form or shape
(having no form or mark)
— only that understands how to expound the Dharma and listen to the Dharma. What is called that which is without form or shape is precisely your own self-nature."
The Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka says:
"It is like a wooden man or a reanimated corpse
(a corpse made to rise and walk about)
, which by the force of the pisacha's mechanism moves and turns, so that its speech and action
(words and deeds)
never cease."
This is saying: the physical body is like a wooden man or a corpse; it speaks and acts by the force of a mechanism. That mechanism is the vital life-force that is the self-nature.

To be attuned to the self-nature is to feel this living vitality within the body, to become one with it, and to abide steadily in it. When you are attuned to the self-nature, deluded thoughts do not arise, and you can effortlessly and naturally attain no-thought, or single-minded thought. To be attuned to the self-nature continuously and without interruption is to be aware of and feel, at all times and in all places, the living vitality of the self-nature within the body, to become one with it, and to abide in it. In daily life, when conditions come, give; when conditions go, be still. Whether you are working or conversing, keep yourself attuned to the self-nature, free and in command (not falling into deluded thought, not manipulated by circumstances and conditions).

Ordinarily, people are inseparable from the "I" of the five aggregates of body and mind; this is the state of delusion. When you leave that "I" behind and are attuned to the self-nature, this is the state of enlightenment. Not leaving the "I" of the five aggregates of body and mind is delusion, and it creates the karma of rebirth; whereas leaving that "I" behind and being attuned to the self-nature is enlightenment, and it plants a great field of merit and constantly gives rise to wisdom. The Formula for Cultivating the Mind says:

"Those who awaken to this and guard it abide in the one suchness and are unmoved in liberation; those who are deluded about this and turn from it journey through the six destinies and undergo kalpas of rebirth."
(See in full
A Detailed Explanation of the Formula for Cultivating the Mind
[Abiding in the one suchness] "To sit": to hold fast. "One suchness": "one" means not two; "suchness" means not different. Not two and not different is called the one suchness.
The more deeply you peer into it, the more deeply you are attuned to the essence itself.
Master Yinguang's Record of Groping for the Elephant in the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation says:
"Layer upon layer investigate the essence; earnestly and urgently keep it alert."
(Translation: continuously and ever more deeply be attuned to the self-nature, and earnestly and vigilantly sustain right mindfulness.)
[Keep it alert] Vigilantly sustain right mindfulness. Master Lianchi says:
"I pray you let go of the ten thousand conditions, and through the twelve hours
(the twenty-four hours)
of the day keep it alert in every thought — this is my utmost hope."
(Yunqi's Dharma Collection) The Gateless Gate of the Chan School says:
"Take the three hundred and sixty joints and the eighty-four thousand pores of the whole body and raise a mass of doubt through them all; investigate the word 'wu' and keep it alert day and night."
When your attunement deepens, you will feel that within there is a deep, vast, boundless space that is still and yet knowing.
To dwell in it without losing your awareness is to dwell in the pure, luminous essence of the true mind. The Buddha says:
"From beginningless time all sentient beings have continued in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous essence of nature
(all because they do not know that they permanently abide in the pure and luminous essence of the true mind)
, and so they employ deluded thoughts
(and take up deluded thoughts instead)
; these thoughts are not real, and therefore there is turning about."
(The Surangama Sutra)

[The pure and luminous essence of nature] The luminous and wondrous essence whose nature is fundamentally pure. "Pure in nature": the nature is fundamentally pure, free of bondage and defilement. "Luminous essence": the luminous and wondrous essence itself. [The pure and luminous essence of the true mind] Grammatically, "the pure and luminous essence of nature" is an appositive that qualifies the noun "true mind." [Turning about] Fragmented birth and death, and transformational birth and death. [Fragmented birth and death] Sentient beings within the three realms and six destinies, because of the good and evil karma they have created, all have a limited lifespan and a body marked out by segments; hence their birth and death is called "fragmented birth and death." One who ends fragmented birth and death escapes rebirth. [Transformational birth and death] For sages of the three vehicles (the hearer vehicle, the solitary-realizer vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle), who have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended fragmented birth and death, in the course of cultivating the path deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each stage of this shift from delusion to awakening differs from the last, and the passage from the previous stage into the next is exactly like one round of birth and death. Its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable; hence it is called "transformational birth and death." One who ends transformational birth and death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit.
The reason for saying that "if a deluded thought arises, you should immediately raise a single Buddha-name (or huatou)" is that this has three functions:
1. Buddha means awakened. To raise a single Buddha-name is to warn yourself to be awake and not deluded;
2. It reminds you to gather your spirit at once and turn the light around to shine back, single-mindedly and continuously peering into who is reciting the Buddha;

3. If you already have some skill in reciting the Buddha-name, then the moment the Buddha-name is raised, deluded thoughts vanish entirely. Thereupon you slip free of deluded thought, creating the conditions for the feeling of doubt (peering without thought) to arise.

Take special note that investigating "who is reciting the Buddha" has a pitfall: treating "who is reciting the Buddha" as a huatou, and using the conscious mind to ponder and conjecture who it is that recites the Buddha, who on earth it is. You take deluded thought for the feeling of doubt, conjure up some fine scenery, and then declare yourself enlightened. This is not investigation but deluded thinking, and it runs counter to illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
On this point, Elder Master Xuyun gave this instruction:

"Therefore the huatou 'who' is truly a wondrous method of Chan investigation. But it is not to recite the word 'who' or the four words 'who is reciting the Buddha' as though they were a Buddha-name, nor is it to ponder and conjecture, seeking out who it is that recites the Buddha — that is what is called the feeling of doubt. There are some
(certain people)

who never stop reciting the four words 'who is reciting the Buddha' with their mouths; better to recite a single Amitābha Buddha, whose merit is greater. There are others who think wildly, searching east and west, and call that the feeling of doubt; they do not realize that the more they think, the more deluded thoughts multiply — like trying to rise and instead falling. You must know this."
(Elder Master Xuyun's Informal Instructions,
Chan Hall Instructions
Therefore investigation must be carried out apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness (see in full
Investigating Apart from Mind and Consciousness
The core of investigation:
take good care of the feeling of doubt
(peering without thought)
, and never neglect it day or night.

As long as you take good care of the feeling of doubt in this way, your power of awareness will rise swiftly, becoming ever more focused, continuous, and enduring. Once awareness is no longer interrupted by subtle thoughts, the original nature stands fully revealed, and you have illuminated the mind and seen the nature.

Question: Why is it that when I gather my spirit and turn the light around to shine back, peering single-mindedly and continuously, deluded thoughts still remain, and deluded thoughts and peering run along side by side at the same time?

Answer: This is because your peering is in fact not yet continuous and has not yet joined into stretches, so moments of peering and moments of deluded thought alternate, and you mistake this for the two running side by side. This is a common situation in the beginning stage. So the first task in beginning practice is, through constant exercise of "gathering the spirit, turning the light around to shine back, and peering single-mindedly and continuously," to join peering into stretches. Once peering forms stretches, within those brief stretches there are naturally no deluded thoughts. Then the feeling of doubt (peering without thought) stands before you and gains a foothold. After that, it is a matter of having no deluded thoughts between huatous (Buddha-names) over long stretches of time. When this step is accomplished, you have attained the ten thousand thoughts returning to one. Further, cause the feeling of doubt to lengthen and endure, accumulating by fractions of an inch until they make a foot, until it becomes a piece, becomes a mass. Until not a single thought arises and only the feeling of doubt remains. This is the state of the one returning to nothing.
If deluded thoughts swarm thickly and you find it very hard

to join peering into stretches, this shows that your power of awareness is weak. I suggest you first study and practice according to the "Preliminaries" chapter above, and only begin investigation once the foundation is laid. The more solid the foundation, the smoother and more effective the later practice will be.
Question: According to the records, Master Yuexi asked Elder Tieshan, "By what method should I apply effort if I am to illuminate the mind and see the nature?" Elder Tieshan replied:

"You must not go and cut off deluded thoughts. Use the eye-faculty to look back toward where there is neither being nor non-being, toward that dark deep pit. Do not let it be interrupted while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. When the time and conditions come, when with a crash the limpid darkness of that dark deep pit breaks open, then you can illuminate the mind and see the nature."

When the master (Master Yuexi) heard these words, it was as though he drank sweet dew. From then on he applied himself day and night, investigating bitterly, until his face grew gaunt and he was thin as firewood. Then one midnight, hearing the sound of the wind blowing the leaves of the wutong tree outside his window, he suddenly had an awakening." Why did Elder Tieshan say, "You must not go and cut off deluded thoughts"?

Answer: The essential point of Elder Tieshan's instructed method is: "Use the eye-faculty to look back toward where there is neither being nor non-being, toward that dark deep pit, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
without interruption

." The meaning of "you must not go and cut off deluded thoughts" is: do not put your attention on cutting off deluded thoughts, but place it wholly on looking back (what is called "looking back" is peering inward). In fact, as long as you look back with focus and continuity, deluded thoughts naturally cease. Moreover, as long as you continue looking back with focus and continuity, no further deluded thoughts will arise. If a deluded thought does arise, this shows that the looking back has been interrupted through slackness; so again do not go and cut off the deluded thought, but rouse your spirit and once more look back with focus and continuity, and the deluded thought ceases of itself. Therefore the essential point of applying effort in this method is: with focus, continuity, and endurance, "use the eye-faculty to look back toward where there is neither being nor non-being, toward that dark deep pit, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
without interruption
." As days pass and your skill deepens, when the melon is ripe the stem falls of itself, and with a crash the dark deep pit breaks open and you see the nature thoroughly.

[Without interruption while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down] The "without interruption" spoken of here means not only that you should not stop the looking back, but that even while looking back you should be focused and continuous and must not be interrupted through slackness.

Investigating the Buddha-recitation has three stages: only the Buddha-name remains (the ten thousand thoughts returning to one), not a single thought arises (the one returning to nothing), and illuminating the mind and seeing the nature (personally realizing the original nature).
On these three stages, Master Hanshan gave this instruction:
"In the gong-an of examining the Buddha-recitation into reality
(investigating the Buddha-recitation)
, one simply raises a single Amitābha Buddha as the huatou
, and at the very place of raising it, at once brings down the feeling of doubt, examining who
(this one)

is reciting the Buddha. Raise it again and examine again, examine and examine once more, to see who on earth it is that recites the Buddha. Settling thus upon the huatou, all deluded and miscellaneous thoughts are cut off at once, like cutting through a tangled skein of silk; they are no longer allowed to arise, and wherever they arise they dissolve.
There is only a single thought, vivid and clearly alone
