, like the white sun in the empty sky; deluded thoughts do not arise, dullness recedes of itself, still and yet awake.
When you see
(peer into)
the place where not a single thought arises, then the former and latter limits are cut off, and the middle stands alone
Suddenly the black lacquer bucket is smashed, and you at once see the original face
. Then body, mind, and world sink level in that instant
(the same as "sink")
, like the falling shadows of flowers in space
(the phantom shadows of flowers in space cease)
, and the ten quarters are perfectly bright, forming one great treasury of light.
Only thus is it the season of arriving home

, present before you in daily use, bright and perfectly clear, beyond all doubt. Only then do you trust that your own mind is of itself thus. The buddhas and patriarchs of old, in their own personal enjoyment, are no different and no other."
(Dream Roaming Collection
Essential Instructions on Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation; for the full text and its annotations see in full
The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
·Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation
[Examining who (this one) is reciting the Buddha] This "examining" is not examining with mind, intellect, and consciousness (discursive thought), but examining by
peering
. Master Hanshan says:
"In speaking now of investigating the Buddha-recitation, the intent is wondrous awakening
(illuminating the mind and seeing the nature)
, and this is done by taking a single utterance of the Buddha as a huatou to investigate — what is called the gong-an of reciting the Buddha and investigating Chan.
Simply raise a single utterance of the Buddha, and at once doubtfully examine who it is.
Peer deeply into it

: from where does this Buddha arise, and who on earth is it that recites? Doubt on and on in this way, investigate and investigate again; after a long time the effort takes hold, and suddenly you awaken
(illuminate the mind and see the nature)
(Dream Roaming Collection: Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)

[Former and latter limits] The former limit refers to the past, the latter limit to the future. The Jingying Commentary says: "Conditioned dharmas arise one after another, front and back. The front is the former limit, the back is the latter limit." [Former and latter limits cut off, the middle stands alone] With no former thought and no latter thought, the state of awareness that is alone and vivid — that is, the state in which not a single thought arises. The Record of the Mirror of the School says:

"Thus the Heart Essentials Annotated says: if not a single thought arises, then the former and latter limits are cut off. The substance of illumination stands independent; things and self are both suchness, directly reaching the source of mind."
The Preface to the Collected Interpretations of Chan Sources says:
"Hearing once, one awakens to a thousand things and gains the great dharani; not a single thought arises, and the former and latter limits are cut off."
[Sink level]
Also written "sink level": to disappear.
In this passage of instruction,
"there is only a single thought, vivid and clearly alone"
— this is the ten thousand thoughts returning to one
(only the single thought of the huatou)
"when you see the place where not a single thought arises, then the former and latter limits are cut off, and the middle stands alone"
— this is the one returning to nothing
(even the single thought of the huatou is gone)
"Suddenly the black lacquer bucket is smashed, and you at once see the original face"
— this is illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
"Body, mind, and world sink level in that instant, like the falling shadows of flowers in space, and the ten quarters are perfectly bright, forming one great treasury of light"
— this is a depiction of the state of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
"Only thus is it the season of arriving home"
— this states that the aim of investigation is to illuminate the mind and see the nature
(to personally realize the original nature)
. And after illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, what follows is the work of protection and maintenance.

Note: After "not a single thought arises (the one returning to nothing)" this essay adds a section on "equal upholding of samādhi and prajñā," in order to help you maintain the non-arising of a single thought amid all circumstances and conditions.
(1) Only the Buddha-Name Remains (the Ten Thousand Thoughts Returning to One)
Deluded thoughts are your sparring partner — let the storm come all the more fiercely!

Only the Buddha-name remains means that there is only the Buddha-name (the huatou) and the feeling of doubt, with no other thoughts: this is the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one. "Only the Buddha-name remains" is also called thought after thought in succession: the Buddha-name (the huatou) is not interrupted by deluded thoughts (though there need not be no interval of time between one Buddha-name and the next).
Method:
raise a single Buddha-name (Amitābha Buddha), and at once gather your spirit to peer inward
(attuned to the self-nature)

: who is reciting the Buddha? After a while, if a deluded thought arises, raise a single Buddha-name again, and again gather your spirit to peer inward in the same way: who is reciting the Buddha? If no deluded thought arises, then simply keep peering.
The essential point
is this:

recite and peer, peer deeply, peer continuously. Until the Buddha-name is vivid and distinct, neither dull nor scattered. This is the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, which is also the state of single-mindedness unmoved in the Pure Land school.
[Neither dull nor scattered] Not sluggish, not scattered (no deluded thoughts).
Master Yinguang described it thus:

"The moment a Buddha-name is raised, deluded thoughts vanish entirely. A coolness penetrates the whole body, joy fills the breast, exactly like sweet dew poured over the crown, like ghee anointing the mind. Its bliss cannot be described."
(Record of Groping for the Elephant in the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation)

Translation: The moment a Buddha-name is raised, deluded thoughts vanish entirely. A coolness penetrates the whole body, joy fills you, as though sweet dew (the water of wisdom) were poured over your crown and ghee (the supreme Dharma) anointed your mind. Truly there is nothing to compare with the bliss of reciting the Buddha!
Zhongfeng's Three Periods of Recitation says:

"Raise a single utterance of the Buddha's name, and straightaway there is no other seeing. Like the Tai'e sword laid across the palace gate; like a great fire-wheel, leaping with blazing flame. All things that touch it are scorched, all that brush it are burned. Until single-mindedness unmoved, with both the able and the object forgotten."
Master Hanshan says:
"Thus
settling upon the huatou
(the Buddha-name)
, all deluded and miscellaneous thoughts are cut off at once, like cutting through a tangled skein of silk; they are no longer allowed to arise, and wherever they arise they dissolve
(the moment they arise, you must at once raise the Buddha-name to wipe them out)
There is only a single thought
(the Buddha-name)
, vivid and clearly alone
, like the white sun in the empty sky; deluded thoughts do not arise, dullness recedes of itself, still and yet awake."
(Dream Roaming Collection
Essential Instructions on Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation)
There is only a single thought, vivid and clearly alone" — this is the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one.
If the mind is deluded, recite the Buddha at once. The moment the Buddha-name is raised, you are at once awake
(the moment the Buddha-name is raised and deluded thoughts are cut off, this is awakening)

. Being awake, the self-nature's light stands forth alone in its brilliance, and all kinds of deluded thoughts instantly melt like ice. Once the karmic defilement is dissolved, the mind of itself is pure and utterly free of burden. Free of burden, suffering ceases and joy remains, calamity departs and blessing arrives.
Question: After reading
One-Minute Chan
, I feel great admiration for this one-minute chan. May I ask how it can be done?

Answer: This one-minute chan can be done by anyone; it is also the minimum requirement of investigating the Buddha-recitation and must be achieved. The method is: raise a single Buddha-name, and at once peer deeply inward: who is reciting the Buddha? Keep practicing, and at first a brief thought-free gap will appear; then the thought-free time will gradually lengthen, until raising a single Buddha-name sustains more than a minute of no-thought. This state of stillness and yet knowing (thought-free yet aware) is what the school calls the former and latter limits cut off; it is chan samādhi. On the webpage of
One-Minute Chan
there is an audio recording of the bell striking after one minute
, and you can practice along with it.

Then practice this one-minute chan under all kinds of circumstances, especially when joy, anger, sorrow, or happiness arise, and when gain and loss, love and hate, affection and enmity assail your mind: raise a single Buddha-name, and at once not a single thought arises (there is only deep inward peering), sustained for one minute.
This one-minute chan led by the Buddha-name is the kingly vajra sword that cuts off deluded thoughts. Refine it and
(apply it)
until it is utterly familiar, and what fear is there that at the end of life you will not be reborn in the Pure Land!
In
One-Minute Chan
there is this passage:

"Try it many times each day, and in time you will of yourself attain the state of still extinction and ease. Then the original face is naturally realized, and the three powers of samādhi, prajñā, and emptiness are naturally awakened. The only fear is that you will not do it. If you can steal a moment from your busyness and do it once, becoming familiar once, then you can be in chan at every moment and recite the Buddha at all times, until it becomes one continuous piece.
On that final day, you will of yourself be clear in right mindfulness
. The terror in your mind and the pain in your body will at once be released, because old debts and past karma have already been paid off one by one,
and you may even foreknow the time of your passing
. Among my companions, there are already many whose word is reliable and verified
(among the friends who practice this one-minute chan, there are already many who truly foreknew the time of their passing and were clear in right mindfulness at the end)

[Companions] Also written "colleagues": those who work together or belong to the same calling. [Whose word is reliable and verified] Those who have truly verified it. Reliable means certain; verified means confirmed and proven.

Moreover, when a deluded thought arises, this is karma binding the mind; to replace it with the Buddha-name is the mind turning karma. This one-minute chan led by the Buddha-name is a sharp instrument for turning karma by mind. In the circumstances and conditions of daily life, use it at all times and in all places to turn defiled karma into pure karma. Persist in this, and defiled karma decreases day by day while pure karma increases day by day.
Once pure karma is accomplished, you can foreknow the time of your passing.
(Further reading:
Turning Karma by Mind

[Defiled karma and pure karma] The world's good and evil karma is defiled karma (the karma of rebirth), which at the end of life draws the consciousness into the six destinies. Good karma draws one into the three good destinies (gods, humans, asuras); evil karma draws one into the three evil destinies (animals, hungry ghosts, hells). Single-minded Buddha-recitation is pure karma, which at the end of life evokes Amitābha Buddha to come and receive you, so that you are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Good karma, evil karma, and pure karma are like a man's debts: the stronger creditor draws him first. [The stronger creditor draws him first] At the end of life, whichever karma is stronger is the karma whose retribution you receive first.
In Pure Land or Chan? there is a splendid question:

"Question: The practice of thought after thought in succession is surely what I wish for. But alas, samādhi-power is not yet accomplished and the thoughts have no master. Either old habits of study are not forgotten; or perverse thinking stirs wildly; or when circumstances and conditions touch me, I cannot keep watch firmly; or feelings and imaginings fly about and cannot be held back. Without noticing it, my thoughts run east and west, and in the blink of an eye they are a thousand miles away. Or if I am caught by the slightest worldly matter, then five days or ten, half a month or a month go by and I cannot shake it off — and that is not merely interruption! To speak of it is shameful, to think of it is heartbreaking. What strategy is there to deal with this?"
[Heartbreaking (tong)] Utterly sorrowful, weeping aloud.
I hope that through the actual practice of the one-minute chan you will prove:
this one-minute chan is the answer to "what strategy is there to deal with this
When the ten thousand thoughts returning to one is roughly accomplished, then please read
The Mind Can Turn Karma

, and by turning karma through mind, solidify the skill of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one. In this way karma turns and destiny turns, and single-mindedness unmoved is likewise accomplished.

Ordinarily, when people sleep at night, before falling asleep they are all indulging in deluded thoughts. This not only wastes time and harms the body, but also creates the karma of rebirth. Make a firm rule for yourself: before falling asleep, always investigate the Buddha-recitation. If you wake in the middle, at once continue investigating the Buddha-recitation until you fall asleep again.
Turn this rule into a habit and make it second nature; this is a powerful guarantee of ending birth and death.
Through the study and practice of this stage,
you will truly attain single-minded Buddha-recitation
(reciting the Buddha without deluded thoughts).
This is the field for choosing buddhas; return home with single-mindedness and you pass the rank.
[Pass the rank] To be selected in an examination.
Single-minded Buddha-recitation is supremely excellent.
For single-minded Buddha-recitation fulfills all three trainings of precepts, samādhi, and prajñā:

Precepts guard against faults: if you can recite the Buddha with single-mindedness, then all evils do not enter, and that is precepts. Samādhi removes scatteredness: if you recite the Buddha with single-mindedness, the mind does not climb after anything else, and that is samādhi. Prajñā is clear illumination: if you contemplate the Buddha-name until every word is distinct, and also observe that both the one who recites and the one recited are unobtainable, that is prajñā. Therefore single-minded Buddha-recitation is itself precepts, samādhi, and prajñā.

[The three trainings] The training in precepts, the training in samādhi, and the training in prajñā. Precepts are the prohibitive discipline taught in the Vinaya pitaka, which can prevent people from committing any evil karma of body, speech, and mind; samādhi is chan concentration, taught in the sutra pitaka, which can calm the mind and clarify it in quiet contemplation; prajñā is wisdom, taught in the abhidharma pitaka, which enables people to discover the truth and cut off foolishness. Cultivating these three trainings, one may attain samādhi through precepts, and give rise to prajñā through samādhi, finally gaining the flawless fruit of the path; hence the three trainings are also called the "three flawless trainings."
For single-minded Buddha-recitation fulfills the six perfections and all practices:

In single-minded Buddha-recitation, the ten thousand conditions are naturally let go — this is the perfection of giving; in single-minded Buddha-recitation, all evils naturally cease — this is the perfection of precepts; in single-minded Buddha-recitation, the mind naturally grows gentle — this is the perfection of patience; in single-minded Buddha-recitation, one never falls back — this is the perfection of effort; in single-minded Buddha-recitation, no other thoughts arise — this is the perfection of samādhi; in single-minded Buddha-recitation, right mindfulness is distinct — this is the perfection of prajñā. Extending this to every practice, in single-minded Buddha-recitation all practices are fulfilled.

[The six perfections] The six gates by which one crosses from this shore of birth-and-death affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa's peace and bliss: giving, precepts, patience, effort, samādhi, and prajñā. Giving crosses over stinginess and greed; precepts cross over transgression; patience crosses over anger; effort crosses over laziness; samādhi crosses over scatteredness; prajñā crosses over foolishness. [The six perfections and all practices] The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
"Then, through three asamkhyeya kalpas
(three great asamkhyeya kalpas)
, cultivating the six perfections and all practices, all perfectly fulfilled, one then realizes the Buddha-fruit."
Therefore single-minded Buddha-recitation is a gate of great bliss and great liberation. Let go of the ten thousand conditions, recite the Buddha with single-mindedness, and attain great freedom.
Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, gave this instruction:
To recite Amitābha's name with single-minded
concentration, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long or short the time,
never letting go of it thought after thought
(each thought not drawn away by deluded thoughts)
— this is called
the karma of definite samādhi
because it accords with that Buddha's
(Amitābha Buddha's)
vow

blocks.text: (2) Not a Single Thought Arises (the One Returning to Nothing)

inline.s: Not a single thought arises: there is only the feeling of doubt and no huatou. This is the state of the one returning to nothing.
Not a single thought arises
] What is here called "
not a single thought arises
" is
having only the feeling of doubt and no huatou

, that is, only peering and no other thoughts. In fact, peering is itself a thought, but it is the key to illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, and it is exceedingly precious. When only the single thought of peering remains, true doubt stands before you. Practice it long, and this single thought of peering suddenly snaps apart, mind and object both perish, and you illuminate the mind and see the nature. [Mind and object both perish] The mind that peers and the object peered into are extinguished together — the able and the object both perish.

Method: raise a single Buddha-name, and at once gather your spirit to peer inward: who is reciting the Buddha? After a while, if a deluded thought arises (or when the peering slackens), raise a single Buddha-name again, and again gather your spirit to peer inward in the same way: who is reciting the Buddha? If no deluded thought arises, then simply keep peering. First, skillfully make the interval between two Buddha-names no less than one minute; this is the one-minute chan led by the Buddha-name spoken of earlier. This is a most important foundation, and you must train strictly against a clock (you may also use the audio player in the article
One-Minute Chan
), and the skill must be fine, dense, and solid. Then, on this basis, gradually lengthen the interval between two Buddha-names.

[The one-minute chan led by the Buddha-name] Begin with raising a single Buddha-name and sustaining five seconds of no-thought, or ten seconds of no-thought, or twenty seconds of no-thought; do this often, gradually lengthening it, until one minute of no-thought, and even longer. The secret of practice is: divide one great step into a number of small steps, advance in order, neither rushing nor neglecting, continuously and without break, seizing every opening.

Practicing thus, when your skill runs deep, at this point raising a single Buddha-name will make the feeling of doubt (peering without thought) endure in an unbroken flow, and you need no longer raise the Buddha-name again (or you may occasionally raise a single Buddha-name as needed), but single-mindedly take good care of the feeling of doubt,
peering into the place before a single thought has sprouted
. This is the state of the one returning to nothing (not a single thought arises).
Peering into the place before a single thought has sprouted — this is the very marrow of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
The task of this stage is: take good care of the feeling of doubt,
do well the work of peering without thought
Earnestly and urgently keep it alert; do not let it be interrupted
. The work must grow finer and denser.

The moment a deluded thought arises, at once be aware and remove it. Practicing thus for a long time, motion and stillness become one piece, and when the mind that observes and the object observed both perish (the able and the object both perish), you see the nature thoroughly.
[Keep it alert] Vigilantly sustain right mindfulness; the right mindfulness spoken of here is peering. Master Lianchi says:
"I pray you let go of the ten thousand conditions, and through the twelve hours
(the twenty-four hours)
of the day keep it alert in every thought — this is my utmost hope."
(Yunqi's Dharma Collection)

[At once be aware and remove it] If a deluded thought arises, it is because the peering has slackened or even been lost; then with a stern jolt of awareness, peer with focus, and the deluded thought ceases.
Remember:
Deluded thoughts arise in the gaps of peering, and blaze up when peering is forgotten.

You may also extinguish deluded thoughts in this way: when a deluded thought arises, at the very place of its arising and ceasing, peer fixedly upon it with a single peer, and watch where it arises from and where it ceases to. Press hard upon it thus with one squeeze (za, to press and crush); whatever deluded thought it may be, one squeeze shatters it to bits, and in that instant it melts like ice and crumbles like tiles. Never follow it along, and never let it continue.

When a deluded thought arises, this is karma binding the mind; be aware of it and it is gone, for this is the mind turning karma. Persist in this, and when your skill runs deep, you will be able to remain for long periods in the state of "not a single thought arising," and even if a deluded thought occasionally arises, it will drift away and vanish (what is called "a flake of snow in a red-hot furnace"); further, you will remain for long periods in
the thought-free state of

"not a single thought arising," and know clearly that it is thought-free — what is called "still and yet illumining, illumining and yet still"; until motion and stillness become one piece. The ancient worthies say:
"At this point it is like moonlight shining through water
(at this time, the mass of doubt is like the moon's reflection in water)
, and on a rushing rapid, amid tumbling waves, it is not scattered by the touch nor lost in the tossing, but lives leaping and alive."
(Encouragement in the Chan Pass)
[Leaping and alive
bo bo
] The appearance of being vividly alive.

This state (still and yet illumining, illumining and yet still, motion and stillness become one piece) is dwelling stably in the state of "such a time"; it is the prelude to enlightenment — what is called drilling wood to make fire, the time when smoke flies. Mr. Liu Zhuyuan says:
"If in a single day one can dwell in the mind thus for several hours
(peering without thought. If one is thought-free without peering, one falls into empty oblivion, and this is not the feeling of doubt)
, only then does it accord with the method.
Of itself there will come the causal condition that sets it off
, and there is no need for anyone to guide you.
The patriarch says: 'If only you can be at such a time, you need not worry that you will not awaken thoroughly.'"
(The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma)
[Sui
sui
] An ancient device for making fire
. [The time when smoke flies] When thick smoke flies, fire will soon follow. [Such a time] When the Sixth Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to Huiming, he said:
"Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at the very moment of such a time
(at this juncture when not a single thought arises)
, what is the original face of Venerable Ming
(which is your original face)
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch) Mr. Liu Zhuyuan says:
"Yet of this gong-an
("Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at the very moment of such a time, what is the original face of Venerable Ming?")

, the most important thing is the three characters 'such a time'; they are the secret of the Chan school. If a person of aspiration can dwell in the mind thus, then awakening is not far off. The patriarch says: 'Such a time is called the time before the Buddha was born.' It is also called: 'Dwelling at the summit, precious beyond compare.' If in a single day one can dwell in the mind thus for several hours, only then does it accord with the method. Of itself there will come the causal condition that sets it off, and there is no need for anyone to guide you. The patriarch says: 'If only you can be at such a time, you need not worry that you will not awaken thoroughly.' This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind-dharma; you may put it into practice with vigor."
(See in full
The Mind Essentials of Baiyun
Mazu says:

"A single deluded thought is the root of birth and death within the three realms; but when there is not a single thought, the root of birth and death is removed, and you gain the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma King."
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi)
The Sutra on the Method of Contemplating Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:

"The ocean of all karmic obstacles arises entirely from deluded thought. If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark. All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them."
Master Hanshan says:
"A mind without things is the true mark."
(See in full
Dissolving Old Karma

) A mind in which not a single thought arises is a mind without things. Through the study and practice of "not a single thought arises" at this stage, you already possess the capacity to extinguish offenses and remove obstacles, and you must put it to real use amid circumstances and conditions. Please read
The Three No's: No-Thought, No-Mark, No-Abiding
, and let the work of not a single thought arising grow ever more perfect and mature in the process of extinguishing offenses and removing obstacles.
On how to
illuminate the mind and see the nature, Master Hanshan gave this instruction:

"How is it that investigation is itself Buddha-recitation, and Buddha-recitation is itself investigation? In investigating nowadays, simply take the single phrase Amitābha as the huatou and do the work of examining into reality. Set down together your own body, mind, and world, along with all your former worldly truths, customary phrases, and Buddhist knowledge and views. Then, from within the empty, still, and silent, strenuously raise a single utterance of Amitābha Buddha, vivid and distinct. At the very moment of raising it, look straight down and peer, examining into reality who it is that recites the Buddha. Bring down the feeling of doubt again
(the 'feeling of doubt' spoken of here is gathering the spirit to look and peer: who is reciting the Buddha?)
, examine and examine again
(the 'examining' spoken of here is looking and peering)
, doubt and doubt again, like a donkey gazing into a well.

[Worldly truth] Also called conventional truth; it means the truth of the world, and also refers to the principles known to worldly people. [Like a donkey gazing into a well] Like a donkey staring stupidly at the water in a well; it illustrates peering beyond feeling and discrimination. The Record of Caoshan says: "The master (Chan Master Caoshan Benji Yuanzheng) asked the senior monk De: 'The Buddha's true dharma-body is like empty space, appearing in forms in response to things, like the moon in water. How would you express the principle of responding (how should this principle be stated)?' De said: 'Like a donkey gazing into a well.' Caoshan said: 'You have only spoken eighty percent of it.' De said: 'And how would you say it, Master (Master, what do you say)?' Caoshan said: 'Like a well gazing at the donkey.'"

"Peering on and peering on, doubting on and doubting on, until you doubt to the place where the path of thought is cut off, like a silver mountain or an iron wall, with no place to turn around or breathe. At that moment, suddenly you knock against it or touch it, and the true no-arising mind
(the original nature)

suddenly appears violently before you. Then sweat pours from your whole body, as if waking from a great dream; only then do you believe that birth is itself no-birth, and no-birth is itself birth, that investigation is itself recitation and recitation is itself investigation. Looking back, you then know that all along you were, as it were, seeking Chang'an from inside the Hanyuan Hall.

[The true no-arising mind] Refers to the original nature. Master Hanshan says: "At first, use the mind to peer and pursue, pursuing until the two ends of a single thought are cut off and the middle stands alone; then toward this solitary place, rouse your finest vigor and pursue straight on, and suddenly the mass of doubt bursts open, and the original face appears of itself — this very thing is the single thought of the true no-arising mind. If a student can only bring this single thought of no-arising before him, then in all places he gains great benefit; this is the season of escaping birth and death." (Dream Roaming Collection: Reply to Prefect Yuan Cangru) [As it were, seeking Chang'an from inside the Hanyuan Hall] The Hanyuan Hall was the main hall of the imperial palace in Chang'an, the capital of the Tang dynasty; "seeking Chang'an from inside the Hanyuan Hall" illustrates being a buddha already while seeking to become a buddha.

"Working thus, what you must most guard against is wanting the mind to awaken. As soon as the mind that wants to awaken is there, it is a board blocking your way. Just keep working straight on, without reckoning the stages. Even when you reach the point where you can work no longer, then rouse your finest vigor
(rouse your spirit)

and start afresh. Again, never crave the mysterious and wondrous. Even if a single thought is temporarily stilled and you feel calm and joyful, never take this as something good; you must spit it out. Never take the mysterious words and wondrous sayings of buddhas and patriarchs as your proof and treat them as the Buddha-dharma; and do not fall into the armor of having nothing to do and take that as attainment.

[Board blocking your way] A plank of wood that blocks the line of sight; it illustrates that the mind wanting to awaken is itself the obstacle blocking the seeing of the path. [The armor of having nothing to do] The armor of having nothing to do; it refers to sitting quietly in emptiness with no deluded thoughts and also no peering. Chan Master Fayen says: "You must rouse your finest vigor, raise a huatou, investigate by day and investigate by night, grappling with it. Do not sit inside the armor of having nothing to do, and do not sit dead on the cushion. If miscellaneous thoughts multiply the more you fight them, gently set them down, get up and walk a round, then return to the cushion. Open both eyes, clench both fists, straighten your backbone, and raise the huatou as before. Then you will feel a coolness, like pouring a ladle of cold water into a boiling cauldron. Working thus, there will surely come the season of arriving home." (The Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs)

"In short, pay no heed to all the holy and ordinary, deluded and awakened; single-mindedly seek where a single thought comes to rest. Pursue it to the place where it is utterly driven out and cut off, and after a long time the original face will appear of itself, like meeting your own father at a crossroads — you will no longer ask anyone where he is. Looking at the matter in this way, it is originally every person's own allotted business, with nothing particularly extraordinary about it. If a cultivator
(a person cultivating the path)
truly takes birth and death as the great matter, let him try to begin here; he will certainly not be deceived."
(Dream Roaming Collection: Instructions to Shen Dajie)

[Like meeting your own father at a crossroads] Like seeing your own father at a crossroads: you recognize him at a glance. It illustrates knowing with certainty that this is the original face, without error. [Deceived] Cheated, fooled.

[The conjured city] A phantom city. It comes from the parable of the conjured city in the Lotus Sutra. The parable of the conjured city says: for all sentient beings, the place of realizing buddhahood is the treasure land; yet the road to this treasure land is perilous and far. The Buddha, fearing that travelers would grow weary and turn back, conjured a city midway, so that they might rest a while, gather their strength, and then press straight on to the treasure land.
At this stage, take special note of two points:
1. If there is no deluded thought and also no peering, but you sit quietly in emptiness, this is soaking a stone in cold water; you may sit for measureless kalpas and gain no benefit.

2. Do not take the conjured city for the treasure land, stopping short at this state of not a single thought arising and refusing to go further. Rather, at the top of a hundred-foot pole, take one more step, and investigate with diligence and vigor until you illuminate the mind and see the nature (see the nature thoroughly).
Chan Master Daoyuan's verse says:
"The one unmoved at the top of a hundred-foot pole
(who has already attained not a single thought arising)
, though he has entered, is not yet genuine; from the top of a hundred-foot pole you must step forward
(see the nature thoroughly)
, and the ten quarters of the world are your whole body."
(The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
[The one unmoved] "Unmoved" means the thoughts do not move (no thought arises), that is, not a single thought arises. "The one unmoved" is a person in whom not a single thought arises.
Chan Master Dahui says:

"Nowadays most people, having gained a state where body and mind are still and extinguished, where the former and latter limits are cut off, where they have put it all down and rested, where a single thought lasts ten thousand years, where they are like the incense burner in an ancient shrine, where they are chilly and cold — take this to be the ultimate; they do not know that they are veiled by this surpassingly wondrous state, so that their own right knowledge and right view cannot come before them, and their spiritual powers and radiance cannot be revealed."
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)

[A single thought lasts ten thousand years] Here "a single thought lasts ten thousand years" describes the ability to maintain for a long period (ten thousand years) the state of a single thought (the ten thousand thoughts returning to one); "rested" means extinguished. "A single thought lasting ten thousand years" is to extinguish even the single remaining thought within the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, and so enter the thought-free state. [Like the incense burner in an ancient shrine] The incense burner of an ancient shrine (the one bit of incense fire left in an ancient shrine): it illustrates a mind pure and undivided — this is the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one. "Like the incense burner in an ancient shrine" (removing even the one bit of incense fire left in the ancient shrine) illustrates passing from the one back to nothing and entering the thought-free state. [A single strip of white silk] White silk: white gossamer. Here white silk likewise illustrates a mind pure and undivided — this is the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one. "A single strip of white silk" means removing even the single remaining thought (the one returning to nothing) and entering the thought-free state.
Elder Master Xuyun gave this instruction:
"There are some
(certain people)

who, because they have reached this state and have a slight grasp of their practice, and have not met with any circumstance they cannot open through, suppose that they have cut off ignorance entirely and that their practice is complete; they do not know that they are living day after day inside the cave of ignorance without even knowing it. If they suddenly meet with a circumstance, they cannot open through it and cannot be master of themselves, but follow it away as before — is this not a great pity! Or there are some who, having reached the state where true doubt stands before them and having gained a little wisdom in the midst of emptiness, and having appreciated a few gong-ans of the ancients, let go of the feeling of doubt and suppose themselves greatly awakened and thoroughly enlightened, composing poems and verses, blinking their eyes and raising their eyebrows, and calling themselves good spiritual friends. Such people mislead themselves and mislead others; their offense is boundless. And there are others who misunderstand the meaning of Old Man Bodhidharma's 'Put to rest all conditions outwardly, let the mind have no panting within, make the mind like a wall, and you may enter the path,' and the Sixth Patriarch's 'Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at the very moment of such a time, what is the original face of Venerable Ming?' — and so take sitting beside a withered tree on a cliff as the ultimate standard. Such people take the conjured city for the treasure land, and mistake a guest's lodging for their native village."
(Elder Master Xuyun's Informal Instructions
Master Hanshan gave this instruction:
"If in this matter
(the path of going beyond)

you do not let go of body and mind and pursue it bitterly to the place where the waters run out and the mountains end, in the end there will be no landing place. Even when you reach the place where the waters run out and the mountains end, the ancients call it the still, sunken
(the same as "sunk")

dead water, and also call it the den of the mysterious and wondrous. If you do not turn your head and reverse your brain, then what lies before you is like an iron wall and a silver mountain: it is only the time of gaining strength, not the place of enjoyment. The ancients applied the mind not by dying all the way to the bottom; they had to come alive within death, and the essential thing was to turn the mechanism and shift the position. Therefore it is said: the one who sits at the top of a hundred-foot pole, though he has entered, is not yet genuine; from the top of the hundred-foot pole step forward once more, and the great thousand worlds reveal your whole body."
(Dream Roaming Collection
Instructions to the Chan Monk Zhuanyu Heng; for annotations see in full
The Instructions of Master Hanshan
[The path of going beyond] The ultimate place of the school (beyond holy and ordinary, out of birth and death) is called the path of going beyond.
Master Hanshan also gave this instruction:

When the ancients applied the mind, they simply settled firmly upon a single phrase of the root huatou, like an iron wall and a silver mountain. If you reach the place where not a single thought arises, this too is a time of gaining strength, but you must not take it as the ultimate. Only when the work proceeds effortlessly, without borrowed thought, and a single thought suddenly opens through, so that body and mind seem to fall into emptiness — only this is the place where the work takes hold, and it too is not yet the ultimate. But if you can reach this, you will naturally be at ease and light, and joy will arise. Yet this is one's own allotted business, not something extraordinary. If you give rise to the notion that it is extraordinary, you fall into the joy-demon and stir up groundless wild knowledge and wild understanding. This pass is the most perilous; this is something the old man
(Master Hanshan's self-reference)
has tested.
The ancients said: 'Before the withered-tree cliff
(a metaphor for the state of not a single thought arising)

there are many wrong roads; travelers who reach here all stumble.' This is no small matter. Even if you have the strength to fight through all kinds of states, that is precisely the time to cultivate and precisely the time to protect; you have not yet arrived home. If you take this as sufficient, then thoughts of the world's various five desires and their causes will arise. This pass is hard to cross; of those who cross it, not one or two in a hundred. Therefore, if you do not reach the ancients' field, it is exactly the fault of being satisfied with little. Even if you, a student, strive bitterly your whole life and reach this place, if you are drawn away by such bad habits, you will still fall into the pit of birth and death, and all your former work will be lost — is this not lamentable!"
(Dream Roaming Collection: Instructions to the Chan Monk Shuanglun Zhao)
Question: When I do the work of peering into the place before a single thought has sprouted, after a long time, or when I do it in the midst of activity, my head grows dizzy. What should I do?

Answer: This shows that your power of awareness is not yet strong enough. Continue the work you were doing before, and when your power of awareness grows strong, then come back to peering into the place before a single thought has sprouted. In the course of training in investigating the Buddha-recitation, whenever you cannot proceed with the work of a new stage, or when discomfort such as dizziness appears, it shows that your power of awareness at that time is not yet equal to the task; then you should continue the earlier training, and only when the power of awareness is equal to the new task should you begin the new stage of training. This is what is meant by filling the hollow and only then advancing.

[Filling the hollow and only then advancing] When spring water meets a hollow, it must fill it before it flows on. This illustrates that cultivation should lay a solid foundation, taking each step firmly, without impatience or reckless advance.
You may also intersperse the training of the new task with the earlier training, gradually increasing the number and duration of the new task each day.

Question: When I peer inward, sometimes it is clear and thought-free. But sometimes it is not clear, and I feel that thoughts seem to flicker in and out. When the latter occurs, should I go and observe the thoughts, doing the work of contemplating the mind?

Answer: This shows that your power of awareness is not yet continuous and stable enough. So the pressing task is: further raise your power of awareness. When the latter occurs, there is no need to observe the thoughts; instead raise a single Buddha-name, and at once peer inward with focus and endurance, peering deeply (clearly illumining the essence, prajñā perfuming ignorance); after a while, raise a single Buddha-name again, ......; and continue in this way. Once the power of awareness rises, the latter situation will naturally disappear.

blocks.text: (3) Equal Upholding of Samādhi and Prajñā

inline.s: All that has marks is delusive
(prajñā)
; do not grasp at marks
, and abide unmoved in suchness
(samādhi)
Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is of itself thought-free; when a thought arises, be aware of it, and being aware of it, it is gone.
If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark; all offenses are like frost and dew, and the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.
An ordinary being of lowly

station, with afflictions blazing, must uphold samādhi and prajñā equally to subdue afflictions and so attain and maintain the state of not a single thought arising. No-thought is samādhi; non-delusion (not taking circumstances and conditions as real, not being entangled by them) is prajñā. To uphold samādhi and prajñā equally is to achieve this: seeing the illusory, at once let it go (knowing it is illusory and not being deluded, not grasping or rejecting out of love and hate — this is prajñā); seeing the illusory, being able to let it go (cutting off deluded thoughts and being thought-free, not giving rise to love and hate, grasping and rejecting — this is samādhi).
[Lowly station (broadly, the ordinary ground)] A humble and inferior position. It refers to the position of lowly ordinary beings.

The essentials of doing the work of upholding samādhi and prajñā equally are: 1. the contemplation of dream-illusion; 2. when a thought arises, be aware of it, and being aware of it, it is gone; 3. let no thought slip past, pass through every thought; 4. dissolve karma and remove offenses.
The
Diamond Sutra says:
"All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated."
It also says:
"All that has marks is delusive."
It also says:
"Do not grasp at marks, and abide unmoved in suchness."

[Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning] As unreal and insubstantial as a dream or an illusion; as instantly vanishing as a bubble or a shadow; as fleeting as morning dew or a flash of lightning. [Abide unmoved in suchness] Not giving rise to habitual reactions, not being entangled.

The contemplation of dream-illusion is to contemplate with all your power amid all circumstances and conditions: all dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning, empty in their very substance; and so not to give rise to habitual reactions, not to be entangled, achieving the not grasping at marks and abiding unmoved in suchness. Step by step, achieve this: awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is of itself thought-free.

[Empty in its very substance] Without waiting for thought or analysis, at once understanding that this is not real, and so abiding unmoved in suchness. A diverting story: the world's first film, Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat, was a short black-and-white silent documentary made by the French Lumière brothers and first shown publicly in Paris on December 28, 1895. This fifty-second silent film showed a steam train drawing into the station of La Ciotat, a small town on the French coast. The audience, terrified by the train rushing straight at them, screamed and fled to the back of the screening room. But who would behave that way now? — This is what is meant by empty in its very substance.
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

"What is ignorance? Good sons! From beginningless time all sentient beings have had all kinds of inversions, like a deluded person who takes the four directions to be reversed, falsely acknowledging the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in space and a second moon. Good sons! Space truly has no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is not only confused about the nature of this empty space, but also deluded about where those real flowers arise. From this false existence, he turns about in birth and death; hence it is called ignorance."

(Translation: What is ignorance? Good sons! From beginningless time all sentient beings, their self-nature deluded and perverted, give rise to all kinds of inversions, taking the false as real — this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he falsely acknowledges the fleshly body formed by the four great elements earth, water, fire, and wind as the mark of his own body, and the phantom reflections appearing when the six faculties contact the six sense objects (the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects) as the mark of his own mind. It is like eyes gone blurry, falsely seeing flowers in space and a second moon. Good sons! In reality there are no flowers in space; this is a phantom clung to by the diseased eye. Because of this false clinging, not only does he falsely cling to empty space as truly existing, but he also thinks that flowers truly arise from there. Because sentient beings, inverted and deluded, falsely acknowledge the illusory body and mind as truly existing and cling to them as self, birth and death turn on without end; hence it is called ignorance.)
This passage of sutra is saying: body and mind (the brain) are illusory, and because sentient beings deludedly cling to body and mind as self (the mark of self), they wander through birth and death.

[The four great elements] All material forms in the world are composed of the four elements earth, water, fire, and wind; hence they are called "great" — the greatness of earth, of water, of fire, of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, wind has movement as its nature. [The shadowy reflections of the six sense objects] The thoughts, feelings, and emotions produced when the six faculties contact the six sense objects: these are phantom reflections cast by the six faculties as they meet the six sense objects, and so they are called the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects; they are also named the mind of clinging and discrimination, which is what people ordinarily call the brain, the mind, or the intellect. [Flowers in space] That is, flowers in the sky. "Flower" is an ancient variant of "blossom."
Always remind yourself:
I am not this body, nor am I this brain
(the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects)

Whenever things go your way or against you, and whenever something circles in your mind and will not leave, you must see through each one of them, see its nature clearly, and not be deceived or entangled by it, not driven by desire, not manipulated by the brain
(the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects)

. The more thoroughly you see through them, the less you suffer and the more free you are. For all suffering comes from ignorance: from taking body and mind to be self, and from taking marks that are wholly illusory to be real — exactly like the terror of being chased by a tiger in a dream.
The
Contemplation of the True Mark of All Dharmas
translated by Master Kumarajiva, Master Hanshan's instruction on life being like a dream (see in full the essay
Life Is a Dream
) and
Master Lianchi's One Stroke to Cross Them Out (see in full the essay
One Stroke to Cross Them Out (with annotations)
) are all models of the dream-illusion contemplation. Read them earnestly and take them to heart,
and at all times verify their principle and apply it in your own life.
In the way you look at all things and events, be compassionate, forgiving, surrendered, and detached.

[Surrender] It means having no resistance in the mind toward events as they are. Having no resistance does not necessarily mean doing nothing at all; it means that no action arises out of habitual reaction. Think it over: which is more effective — action taken in a mood of resentment, or action taken calmly and objectively? Moreover, resistance to events is the root of suffering: the negative emotions and excessive actions it produces usually harm body and mind, career, and human relationships far more than the events themselves do. (See
Case Study: Moving Beyond Suffering
Mr. Jiang Weinong says in his Explication of the Diamond Sutra:
"This unwise one
(a humble way of saying "I")

has studied the Buddha's teaching for twenty years, during which, though I practiced various methods and did various contemplations, I made no progress at all. Then one day, at these four lines of verse
("All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew or a flash of lightning; thus should they be contemplated")
I suddenly seemed to awaken, and I practiced contemplation accordingly. At first it was as if near and as if far, as if clear and as if dim; it did not hold together and was not very effective.
Then I understood that I ought to exert my mind to the utmost in contemplating every circumstance and condition.
However small the matter, and whether the time was most agreeable or most disagreeable, I always sealed it with the principle that all is like a dream and an illusion
— sealed it so

, and likewise sealed the practice of the Buddha's teaching itself with the principle that all is like a dream and an illusion, never departing from this whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. After long practice in this way, though my skill in "not grasping at marks
(wisdom)
" and "abiding in stillness
(concentration)

" is still shallow, it truly began with doing this contemplation. This mind gradually felt empty and void, and toward all circumstances and marks it gradually became unmoved within. When reading sutras my eyes felt a little brighter, and when reciting the Buddha's name I felt a little more grounded. Now I ask you all to try it; you will surely find it useful. You should know that for an ordinary being of this lowly station, who wishes to turn the light around and shine it back, apart from this there is no place to begin the work. Take care! Take care!"

The core of the dream-illusion contemplation is detachment from marks: all marks are illusory; not grasping at marks, one abides in stillness. The deluded cling to marks; the awakened are free of marks.

[Clinging to marks] Taking marks as real and so loving and hating, grasping and rejecting. [Freedom from marks] Realizing that all marks are illusory and so being without love and hate, grasping and rejecting. The Diamond Sutra says:
"All that has marks is illusory. If you see all marks as no marks
(if you see that all marks are not real)
, you see the Tathagata
(that is, you see the Buddha of your own nature)
(For annotations see in full
A Precise Explanation of the Diamond Sutra

blocks.text: 2. When a Thought Arises, Be Aware of It; Being Aware, It Is Gone

inline.s: Master Guifeng says:
"All dharmas are like dreams — the sages all say so
(all the sages say this)
. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the dust of sense objects is originally empty
(like a dream, an illusion)

. This mind of emptiness and stillness, its numinous knowing is not obscured. Just this knowing of emptiness and stillness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not arise through conditions, nor does it arise because of objects. The word "knowing"
(this "knowing" of the knowing of emptiness and stillness)
is the gate of all wonders
(is the gate of all wonders)

. Because of beginningless delusion, one falsely clings to body and mind as self and gives rise to thoughts of greed and hatred. If one meets a good friend who reveals it, one may suddenly awaken to this knowing of emptiness and stillness. This knowing has no thought and no form — who then is the mark of self or the mark of person?
Awaken to all marks as empty, and the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, be aware of it; being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.
Therefore, though one cultivates the ten thousand practices in full,
one takes only no-thought as the foundation
. Once one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought, then liking and disliking
(fondness and aversion)

naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic offenses naturally cease, and one's practice and virtue naturally advance. Having understood that all marks are no marks, one naturally arrives at the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are cut off. When arising and ceasing cease, still illumination appears, functioning without end — this is called Buddha."
(from the Preface to the Collected Interpretations of Chan Sources)

[The knowing of emptiness and stillness] is also called the numinous knowing. [To realize that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought; when a thought arises, immediately be aware of it, and being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies entirely in this.] To realize that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought (this is the dream-illusion contemplation spoken of earlier). If a deluded thought arises, you must at once realize that it is taking illusion as real and being turned by illusory marks. Realizing this, the deluded thought instantly vanishes (this requires the power of concentration to cut off delusion on the spot; the practice is precisely in this). The wondrous gate of practice is right here!
Realizing that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought; when a thought arises, be aware of it, and being aware, it goes away.”
This is the very essence of concentration and wisdom in union!

blocks.text: 3. Not letting go of a single thought, passing through every thought

inline.s: In investigating [the huatou], what is prized is true practice and actual realization, in order to put an end to birth and death. Not letting go of a single thought — that is true practice; passing through every thought — that is actual realization. In daily activity, not apart from a single dharma, not settled in a single dharma, at every point not letting go, passing through each one — this is genuine effort.

[Not letting go] That is, not being deluded by it. [Passing through] That is, not being enveloped by it, not going along with its manipulations, not taking it as a real thing, and still less being held hostage by it.
Master Hanshan instructed:
Practitioners of recent times are ever farther from the sages and do not see the true practice-walk of the ancients,
(that is)

but in the realms manifest in daily use, at the brink of birth and death, pass through each and every one. This very daily use — not apart from a single dharma, not settled in a single dharma, at every point not lightly letting go — is genuine effort. Wherever in the present sounds and forms, favorable and adverse, loved and hated realms, you are able to pass through each one, that is the true gateway of awakening. And in this very awakening, head after head and dharma after dharma, is the real Buddha-dharma.

If you can, at the points in daily use where thoughts arise and stir, where the root of feeling is firmly knotted, where love and hate interlace and are hard to untie, where the habitual tendencies of greed, anger, delusion, and pride are hard to wear away — there, at the very root of the pain, plant an awl
(same as ‘pierce’)
and investigate each and every one to the bottom,
(as dream, illusion, bubble, shadow)
passing through each one,
(cutting off deluded thoughts)
this is true knowledge
(this is to be a true good and wise friend)
; and then at once you ascend to the unhindered, freely at ease, great liberation, the supreme dharma-gate. Apart from this, what other knowledge
(good and wise friend)
is there to consult
(to seek out)
? What more extraordinary dharma-gate is there to enter?”
(See the notes in
True Practice, Real Realization
the essay

In the study of concentration and wisdom in union, there is a very important lesson: seeing is just seeing, hearing is just hearing, being aware is just being aware, knowing is just knowing, without giving rise to thoughts. — Not grasping at marks, still and unmoved in Thusness.
According to the Theravada scripture, the Udana:

There was a practitioner named Bahiya, who after a long, dusty journey arrived at Savatthi to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. Just then he saw the Buddha going door to door in the city for alms, every movement graceful and sublime, with the six sense faculties fully tamed, guarded, and at peace. Bahiya drew near, bowed at his feet, and asked the Buddha to teach him the Dharma — to teach him the Dharma of immeasurable benefit and peace. The Buddha said that he was then going door to door for alms and it was not fitting to teach. But Bahiya pleaded repeatedly, and so the Buddha taught him on the spot:

“Bahiya! You should train thus: in seeing, only what is seen; in hearing, only what is heard; in knowing, only what is known; in being aware, only what is aware. Bahiya! When you can be such that in seeing only the seen, in hearing only the heard, in knowing only the known, in being aware only the aware, then you will have reached freedom from attachment and obstruction. If you are free from attachment and obstruction, then you have no past life and no future life. You have not these two lives of past and future
(but only the present)
; all sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering will thereby be dispersed and vanish.”

[The three times] The past, present, and future. Whatever has arisen and ceased is called the ‘past’; whatever has arisen and not yet ceased is called the ‘present’; whatever has not been born and not yet arisen is called the ‘future’. [But only the present] The scripture says:
“In seeing, only the seen; in hearing, only the heard; in knowing, only the known; in being aware, only the aware.”
and without deluded thoughts about past or future. Indeed, the unease, anxiety, and suffering in people’s minds all arise from deluded imaginings about the past or the future.

blocks.text: 4. Dissolving karma, eradicating offenses, and bestowing blessings

inline.s: The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva says:
“The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born of deluded thought. If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality. All offenses are like frost and dew — the sun of wisdom can dispel them.”
ocean of karmic hindrances
Karmic hindrances as deep and vast as the great sea.
all offenses like frost and dew, the sun of wisdom can dispel them
Just as the sun melts away frost and dew, contemplating reality (the sun of wisdom) can dispel all offenses.
As for “
contemplating reality
”, Master Hanshan explained
“A mind with no things is called reality.”
see
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
, the chapter ‘The Sun of Wisdom Dispels Offenses’)

The mind that is without thought is a mind without things; sitting upright without thought is like the sun melting snow, frost, and dew — dissolving karma and eradicating offenses. This is repentance through reality:

“Offenses arise from the mind, so repent with the mind; when the mind is gone, offenses too are extinguished. When both the mind and its offenses are gone, both are empty — this is called true repentance.”
In the chapter ‘The Sun of Wisdom Dispels Offenses’, Master Hanshan instructed:

[Now, being in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve past karma? One must use the light of wisdom to break through ignorance, and be certain that one’s own mind is originally pure, not driven by deluded, inverted thought; then all karma has no cause, for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about one’s own mind, and life after life, with a deluded mind, created all sorts of karma. These karmic habits accumulate within the field of the eight consciousnesses, watered by the water of ignorance, so that this evil seed sprouts karmic shoots. This is the root of offense, and all evil karma arises from it.]

So now, being in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve past karma? One must use the light of wisdom to break through ignorance, be certain that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by deluded, inverted thought. Then there is no cause for creating karma, for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this? Because from beginningless kalpas one has been deluded about one’s own mind, and life after life, with a deluded mind, created all sorts of karma. These karmic habits accumulate in the alaya-vijnana (the eighth consciousness), watered by the water of ignorance, so that this evil seed sprouts karmic shoots. This is the root of offense, and all evil karma arises from it.
[Now, to dissolve past karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to break through ignorance, not allowing deluded thoughts to sprout and grow in secret.
If you can, at the very point where a deluded thought arises, cut it off with a single thought, then the accumulated root of past karma is dissolved on the spot.

As the saying goes, do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear that awareness is too slow. If awareness comes a little too late, then one is turned by them. If you can, at the points in daily use where thoughts arise and stir, be aware thought after thought and extinguish thought after thought, this is what is meant by ‘all offenses are like frost and dew — the sun of wisdom can dispel them’. Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is what is meant by wisdom being able to dispel them.]
Now, to dissolve past karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to break through ignorance, not allowing deluded thoughts to sprout and grow in secret.
If you can, at the very point where a deluded thought arises, cut it off with a single thought, then the root of karma accumulated in the past is dissolved on the spot.

As the saying goes, ‘do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear that awareness is too slow’. If awareness comes a little too late, then one is turned by it (deluded thought). If you can, at the points in everyday life where thoughts arise and stir, be aware thought after thought and extinguish thought after thought, this is ‘all offenses are like frost and dew — the sun of wisdom can dispel them’. Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is how wisdom is able to dispel all offenses.

[If, day and night without ceasing, you diligently observe and do not let it pass, then right at the place where deluded thought arises, you investigate to the very bottom the mark of non-arising. Looking again and again, in the end it is unobtainable. After a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and your own mind is pure and without things; a mind without things is reality. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought could be accommodated, what accumulated karma could find lodging? This way of using the mind is called the samādhi of contemplation-and-observation.]

You must, day and night without ceasing, diligently observe and not let it pass, but right at the place where deluded thought arises, investigate to the very bottom the mark of non-arising. Looking again and again, the deluded thought is in the end unobtainable. After a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and your own mind is pure and without things,
a mind without things is reality

. If you constantly contemplate this pure mind, what deluded thought could be accommodated, what accumulated karma could find lodging? This way of using the mind is called the samādhi of contemplation-and-observation.

[If, day and night without ceasing, diligently observe] Here ‘ruo’ means ‘you’. For example: ‘If we change your service and restore your levy, then what do you say?’ (This line is from Liu Zongyuan’s ‘The Snake-Catcher’; rendered as: ‘Change your task of catching snakes and restore your tax levy — how would you find that?’)
Master Hanshan further instructed:
“Therefore the Buddha-dharma teaches people, first of all, to
(exclusively to)
make the severing of deluded thought the foundation,
(because)

deluded thought is the root of all manner of evil karma such as greed, anger, and delusion. Even the bodhisattva’s practice leading to Buddhahood, reaping the most sublime, adorned, and vast field of blessings in heaven and among humans, all begins with severing deluded thought.
As
(because)
deluded thought being severed, evil karma is dissolved; evil karma being dissolved, a hundred blessings gather. This is what is meant by seeking abundant blessings for oneself.
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer
for Zhong Hengying)

blocks.text: 4. Both subject and object extinguished (seeing the original nature)

inline.s: Alone the numinous light shines, wholly freed from faculties and dust.

The extinguishing of both subject and object: the mind that observes (investigates) and the realm that is observed (investigated) are together extinguished, and the body, mind, and world at once fade away, while the ten quarters shine all round and bright. This is the state of having thoroughly seen one’s original nature; the Chan school calls it seeing the mind and realizing the nature. For the Pure Land school, this is the attainment of the Buddha-recitation samādhi.
(See
Master Yinguang’s
Groping the Elephant of the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi

[Original nature] The original nature is also called Buddha-nature, the original face, or thusness. Because the original nature is Buddha, it is named Buddha-nature; because the original nature is the primordial state of self-nature, it is named the original face, also abbreviated as the original; because the original nature is unchanging and constant, it is named thusness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The original nature is Buddha; apart from that nature there is no other Buddha.”
For more on the original nature, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
the essay.
Chan Master Baizhang, entering the hall, said:

“Alone the numinous light shines, wholly freed from faculties and dust. The essence is revealed as true and constant, not bound by words and letters. The mind-nature is undefiled, of itself wholly perfected. Only leave the conditions of delusion, and you are the Buddha of Thusness.”
(from the Compendium of the Five Lamps)

[Wholly freed from faculties and dust] The six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and the six sense objects (form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and dharma) are utterly separated. [Conditions of delusion] To cling on one’s own deludedly; here ‘condition’ is a verb. [Only leave the conditions of delusion and you are the Buddha of Thusness] As long as you are free of deluded self-clinging, you are the dharmakāya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
: ‘the Dharma Buddha
(dharmakāya Buddha)
is free from clinging.’
The Diamond Sutra says:
“Free from all marks, this is called being a Buddha.”
[Buddha of Thusness] The Buddha who is awakened to the principle-substance of Thusness, that is, the dharmakāya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“What is the nirmita Buddha? What is the sambhoga Buddha? What is the Buddha of Thusness?”
Master Hanshan said:
“Watch
(investigate)
until you reach the point where a single thought does not arise; then the boundaries of before and after are broken, and the middle stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is smashed,
and you at once see the original face.
Then body, mind, and the world at once sink away
(same as ‘sink’)
, like the shadows of sky-flowers falling
(the illusory shadows of sky-flowers cease)

; the ten quarters shine all round and bright, forming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the time of arriving home; in daily use it is present before you, bright and perfectly clear, beyond all doubt. Only then do you trust that your own mind is of itself thus. The buddhas and patriarchs of old, in their own personal enjoyment, are no different and no other.”
the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer
on the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation
Master Hanshan again said:
“Only within thought after thought,
watch and investigate where thought has not yet arisen.
Because of thus abiding apart from thought, after a long time
(only the single thought of watching and investigating remains)
, suddenly the thought
(the single thought of watching and investigating)
breaks asunder, and mind and realm are both forgotten
(the character is used in the sense of ‘extinguished’)
; like a lion freed from its leash, roaming at ease.”
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer, instructing the Chan practitioner Liaoxin Hai)

[Mind and realm both forgotten (the character is used in the sense of ‘extinguished’)] The mind and realm are both extinguished. This is the state of the extinguishing of both subject and object: the mind that watches and investigates and the realm that is watched and investigated are together extinguished, which is also the state of seeing the mind and realizing the nature.
“The great Way is vast and open, utterly free of thought and reflection.”

The whole process of Chan contemplation is the process of stilling thought. When coarse thoughts are stilled, the ten thousand thoughts return to one; when fine thoughts are stilled, the one returns to nothing (as Elder Xuyun speaks of below as ‘the ten thousand thoughts suddenly stilled’); when the subtlest thoughts are briefly stilled, one sees the mind and realizes the nature.
[The great Way is vast and open, utterly free of thought and reflection] See
The Fourth Patriarch’s Instructions to Farong
the essay. [Coarse thought, fine thought, and subtlest thought]

Mental thoughts are of three kinds: coarse, fine, and subtlest. For example, for a practitioner of Buddha-recitation, a deluded thought is a coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha is a fine thought. Normally, when both coarse and fine thoughts are stilled, that is called no-thought (wunian) — this is what is usually meant by no-thought. Further, if the subtlest thoughts also cease, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore the meaning of the term ‘no-thought’ must be determined from context. For example,
the ‘no-thought’ in ‘the original mind is without thought’ refers to the ultimate no-thought.

[Subtlest thought] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing onward of the consciousness-mind, which is the mark of the alaya-vijnana. When the subtlest thoughts are briefly stilled, one sees the mind and realizes the nature; when the subtlest thoughts are forever stilled,
only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone and remains
, then one fully realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
“When a bodhisattva reaches the end of the grounds
(having fully cultivated the ten grounds)
and perfects the expedient means, then in one instant the awakening-mind first arises and yet the mind has no initial mark;
and because it is far from the subtlest thoughts,
it sees the mind-nature
; the mind is then abiding and constant,
and this is called ultimate awakening.
Master Guifeng said:
If the subtle flowing stream
(the subtlest thoughts)

is wholly stilled and extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone and remains, then answering to conditions it manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies to save sentient beings of karmic affinity,
and this is called being a Buddha.
(see the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era)
In the chronological biography of the Venerable Xuyun, Elder Xuyun recounts his awakening at the age of fifty-six:
The duties within the meditation hall did not assign me
(me)
to watch in turn, so I had the opportunity to practice. From then on
the ten thousand thoughts suddenly stilled
, the effort ‘settled onto the floor,’ day and night as one, and my movements were as swift as flying.

[Settled onto the floor] ‘Settled onto the floor’ means being real and substantial. Elder Xuyun said: ‘Only in Buddha-recitation must you gather the mind to contemplate and observe, every phrase settling onto the floor. To settle onto the floor means being real and substantial. Every phrase real, every thought in accord, and after a long time it naturally becomes one piece.’ (From Fragments of Instruction by Elder Xuyun)

One evening, during the night incense period, I opened my eyes and looked and suddenly saw a great light as bright as day, clear through within and without. Across the wall I saw the incense-lamp master relieving himself, and I saw the West-single master in the latrine
(qing, the latrine)

; and far off, boats moving on the river, and the trees on both banks in all their many colors — all of these I saw clearly. Only then did the three board-strikes sound. The next day I asked the incense-lamp and West-single masters, and indeed it was so. I knew this was a state [of insight] and did not find it strange.
By the eighth retreat of the twelfth month
(the eighth Chan retreat)

, on the third night, when the six-incense period was released from stillness, the attendant of the retreat as usual poured boiling water and it splashed upon my hand, and the teacup fell to the ground. With the sound of breaking, the root of doubt was suddenly cut off, filling my whole life with joy, as if waking from a dream. I thought to myself that in the decades I had wandered since leaving home, at the reed hut by the Yellow River, a common fellow once asked me a question, and I did not know what water was. If at that time I had kicked over the stove
(for what water was there!)
, what would Wen Ji have had to say? Had I not fallen into the water and fallen gravely ill, had I not met the guidance by favorable and adverse means, the good-and-wise friend’s
(good and wise friend)
instruction, I might have missed my whole life; how would there be
(how)
today? Therefore I composed this verse:
The cup falls and strikes the ground; the sound rings out crisp and clear;
Empty space itself is shattered, and the wild mind is at once stilled.
Another verse:
Scalding the hand, smashing the cup; home destroyed, people gone, words hard to speak;
Spring arrives, the fragrance of flowers blooms everywhere; the mountains, rivers, and great earth are the Tathagata.
Preserve: cut off thought and reflection.
Let be: let the mind be at ease and free.
When there is a matter that accords with principle, seeing it, do it; having done it, let it go;
done — what is there not done?

[A matter that accords with principle] Yi means principle and reason. In whatever one undertakes, one should first carefully examine right and wrong and benefit and harm; only when it accords with principle should one then act. This is the mind of waking-awareness, which is different from the mind of wildness and confusion. (See
Karma Cannot Bind

Preserving-and-letting-be (baoren) means preserving and then allowing spontaneous function — these are the two stages of purifying habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. ‘Preserving’ means doing one’s utmost to tend the sage-embryo so that it is not harmed by greed, anger, and delusion, in order to accomplish the first two of the four forbearances (the forbearance of suppression and the forbearance of gentle compliance); ‘letting be’ means that, once the sage-embryo has grown to maturity, following the circumstances and conditions it functions naturally, and is still further refined amid both favorable and adverse conditions, in order to accomplish the latter two of the four forbearances (the forbearance of non-arising and the forbearance of still extinction).

[The four forbearances] The forbearance of suppression, the forbearance of gentle compliance, the forbearance of non-arising, and the forbearance of still extinction. The forbearance of suppression: a beginning practitioner, desiring to endure both favorable and adverse circumstances (without giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion), must first subdue and tame the mind. The forbearance of gentle compliance: having tamed the mind for a long time, when encountering circumstances and conditions, one can endure naturally without forced restraint (without giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion); at this time the mind is gentle, soft, and compliant.
