The forbearance of non-arising: a person of the sage stage realizes that all dharmas are of themselves unarisen; both sentient and insentient things are dependently arisen and without self-nature, empty in their very substance; therefore, in this self-naturelessness, the forbearing mind does not move, and one personally realizes non-arising. The forbearance of still extinction: a sage at the fruit stage who thoroughly realizes the nirvāṇa state of still extinction, where both the mark of movement and the mark of stillness accord with Thusness. [Thusness] The state of self-nature free of inverted discrimination. Because it is the thusness (the true mark of all dharmas) realized by the wisdom that accords with principle, it is called ‘Thusness’.

For one who has been pointed directly to see the nature (found the master of the house), one must first ‘preserve’ and then ‘let be’ — this is what is commonly called sudden awakening with gradual cultivation.

[Direct pointing to seeing the nature] As when Damei asked Mazu, ‘What is the Buddha?’ Mazu replied, ‘This very mind is the Buddha!’ Damei awakened greatly at these words (catching a glimpse of self-nature and finding the master of the house). Again, as when Lingxun asked Master Guizong, ‘What is the Buddha?’ Guizong said, ‘If I tell you now, I fear you will not believe it!’ Lingxun said, ‘The master speaks sincerely; how would I dare not believe!’ Guizong said, ‘You yourself are he!’ Lingxun had an insight at these words (catching a glimpse of self-nature and finding the master of the house).

For one who has passed through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, and the one returning to nothing, and thus seen the mind and realized the nature (thoroughly seeing one’s original nature), this is what is commonly called gradual cultivation with sudden awakening. Since the effort of ‘preserving’ (cutting off thought and reflection — which the Chan community calls ‘the great death’) is already accomplished, one may then devote oneself to the effort of ‘letting be’ (letting the mind be at ease — which the Chan community calls ‘the great life’).
As for how to preserve and let be,
please read
Preserving and Letting Be Along with Conditions
and
The Fourth Patriarch’s Instructions to Farong
these two essays.
Question: What is the Buddha-recitation effort forming into a single piece?
Answer: When reciting the Buddha, do not intermingle deluded thoughts — the thought of reciting continues without interruption to form a single piece. Master Yinguang said:
“If the Buddha-recitation cannot be pure and single, you must restrain the mind so that it does not run outward; after a long time it will of itself become pure and single.
To form into a piece means being pure and without admixture.
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
in the fourth letter to the layman Ma Qixi) Master Hanshan said:
“You must take this single sound of the Buddha
(the Buddha-name)
and hold it fast between your teeth,
and be certain to overcome deluded thought.

In every place, thought after thought, it is present before you, not shrouded by deluded thought. Practicing with such bitter, earnest effort, after a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and it naturally responds — without seeking to form into a piece, it forms into a piece of itself.”
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer,
instructing the layman Jingxin)
Question: What is ‘beating into a single piece’?
Answer:
Master Hanshan instructed:

“If you can truly use the mind, exert effort solely before a single thought arises. After a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and with no thought arising, the original substance manifests before you. The constant light is bright and clear, unshaken in brightness and darkness, one and the same in motion and stillness; only then is it ‘beaten into a single piece’.”
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer,
in answer to the monk Haiyin of Huzhou)
Question: When I am investigating the Buddha-recitation, my deluded thoughts have become far fewer, but when sluggishness strikes I am at a loss. How should I counter sluggishness?

Answer: When sluggishness strikes, you may pause your investigation to counter the sluggishness. The method is: rouse your spirit, at all times raise your head and gaze upward, and do abdominal deep breathing — inhale deeply through the nose (the abdomen protruding) and hold the breath
second, then exhale slowly (the abdomen contracting) and hold the breath
second, keeping each inhale-and-exhale at about

seconds. At the same time, recite the Buddha (on the in-breath recite ‘A-mi’, on the out-breath recite ‘tuo-fo’), and clearly be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen. In this way, the sluggishness will gradually recede. When the sluggishness has gone, return to investigating the Buddha-recitation. You may also adopt the method taught by the ancient worthy in the Chan Pass Policy (compiled by Master Lianchi):
Brothers, having dozed so long on the meditation cushion
(having long sunk into sluggishness)

, you must get down and walk about a while, wash and rinse your mouth with cold water, open your eyes afresh, and then return to the cushion. Straighten up your spine, stand like a cliff of ten thousand fathoms, and lift the huatou single-mindedly.”
In recent times, few are those resolutely devoted to Chan contemplation. No sooner do they investigate a huatou than they are bound by the two demons of sluggishness
(sluggishness)
and scatteredness
(distraction)
; they do not know that sluggishness and distraction are precisely counteracted by the feeling of doubt
(not knowing that the feeling of doubt is precisely the sharp weapon against sluggishness and distraction)
. When faith is strong, the feeling of doubt must be strong; when the feeling of doubt is strong, sluggishness and distraction of themselves vanish.”
One day, in the corridor I met Xiu
(Venerable Xiu)
and was able to draw near to him.
Thereupon I asked: ‘Right now I cannot drive away sluggishness and distraction
(I cannot now get rid of sluggishness and distraction; what shall I do)

.’ Xiu said: ‘You are simply not fierce enough! You must sit high on the cushion, straighten up your spine, and gather your whole body into a single huatou — then what sluggishness or distraction are you still looking for
(where would there still be any sluggishness or distraction)
?’ Following Xiu, I practiced
(so I practiced according to Venerable Xiu’s words)
, and before I knew it both body and mind were forgotten. Clear and pure for three days and nights, my eyes never once closed.”
Throughout the twelve hours, utterly without a thing to cling to
(without the slightest attachment)
, contemplate the one before father and mother were born, which
(which)
one is my original face? Whether it takes effect or not, whether there is sluggishness and distraction or not, just keep lifting it up.”

If there are sluggishness and distraction, do not stir up thoughts to dispel them, but promptly lift up the huatou, rousing body and mind and summoning full vigor. If that does not work, get down and walk in mindful pacing; when you feel the sluggishness and distraction have gone, return to the cushion. Suddenly, without lifting it lifts itself, without doubting it doubts itself. Walking, you do not know you are walking; sitting, you do not know you are sitting. There is only the feeling of investigating, solitary and far-reaching, vivid and clear. This is called the place where afflictions are cut off, and likewise the place where the self is forgotten.”
Question: If the huatou is the word ‘wu’ (no), how should one investigate it?
Answer: If investigating the word ‘wu’, then look inward and investigate: Who is this one who lifts up the word ‘wu’?
Master Hanshan said:

“Single-mindedly raise a single gong-an (public case) as a huatou, such as ‘Zhaozhou: does a dog also have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: No (wu)’, or ‘all dharmas return to one; where does the one return?’, or investigate ‘who is the one reciting the Buddha?’ Whatever one you raise, hold it laid across in your breast like the kingly vajra sword, cutting off in a single stroke all thoughts and deluded imaginings, as one cuts a tangled skein of silk. Within, do not let it out; without, do not let it in. Seal off the vital ford, plug up the throat, and do not allow a breath to escape. Exerting yourself thus,
with a single glance, look: what, in the end, is this one who lifts the huatou?
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer, instructing the mountain master Songpu En)

Question: When I raise a single Buddha-name, I look inward to investigate who is reciting the Buddha. In this way, deluded thoughts become fewer and fewer, and the effort gradually gathers strength. My question is: after investigating this way for a long time, my head grows dizzy; or sometimes I find the practice hard, and if I grit my teeth and keep going, I also grow dizzy. What should I do?

Answer: This shows that your power of awareness is not yet strong enough. You can solve your problem this way: whenever you meet with trouble, such as dizziness and so on, go practice the preliminary practices (
the ‘Preliminary Practices’

chapter). Once you can do it smoothly, then return to your investigation. Persisting in this back-and-forth, the investigating effort will grow more and more powerful, and you will not grow dizzy. At the same time, remember the practical advice on practice: do not rush, and do not stop. Remind yourself of this at all times.

Q: I was investigating my Buddha-name recitation and it was going along just fine. Somehow, I don't know what happened, I've taken a big step backward! No matter what I can't do it well — vexation, weariness, and drowsiness come on one after another, and even deluded thoughts circle around and will not leave. What should I do?

A: This is not a great step backward, but a step forward to the most critical juncture: as your practice gains strength, it presses hard upon the karmic seeds stored in the alaya-consciousness over countless eons and forces them to leap out. You must meet the situation calmly and composedly. The way to deal with it is in a single word:
endure

(“press on against it”). Endure with the warmth and perseverance kindled by genuine faith and earnest vows; once you have endured past it, that is victory! So at this time you must certainly rouse your spirit and never let go of the Buddha-name (the original huatou you are investigating). “You fight your fight, I fight mine” — as long as I keep attending to my own Buddha-name, the boat cannot capsize! Though in enduring you are said to clench your teeth, this chiefly refers to an unshakable faith and the resolve not to bow before difficulty. But in the actual doing, it does not hurt to allow a little humor, and to wear a smile: let's see what you can do to me! Remember, this is the darkness before the dawn. Endure past this pass, and it is a great victory.
press on against (sī ái)
To hold firm against, to press on and hold fast.
The Jade Dew of the Crane Forest says:
“Liao Zihui, holding a minor post, was transferred by his superior on unreasonable grounds, and could not bear it at all. Master Zhu
(Zhu Xi)
wrote to enlighten him, saying: ‘That which we have studied is
precisely what is meant to be tested and revealed here
; already spread out and not drawn back, already advanced and not retreated; one can only, with a stiff spine, press on against it — let's see how it goes!’”
[The karmic seeds over countless eons being pressed hard and forced out] Mr. Jiang Weinong, in his book A Reply to the Layman Mao Jingquan, has this account of experience:
I recall five years ago, this humble one
(Mr. Jiang Weinong speaking of himself)
was in Beijing. One day, just as I was in the middle of reciting the Buddha-name
(one day, just when I was reciting the Buddha-name)
, of a sudden a great evil thought arose; I was terrified beyond measure and my sweat poured out as if washed
(drenched in sweat)
, and for several days I did not dare to do my practice. Afterwards I reflected
(afterwards I thought to myself)
that in all my life I had never had such a thought; whence did this thought come? It must be
(the karmic seeds of many lives
(probably the karmic seeds stored in the alaya-consciousness from many lives past)
, I suppose. Somewhat I let myself off
(somewhat I consoled myself)
. But in the end I was doubtful and could not be sure
(but after all, what on earth it was, I could not determine)
. Later I went to consult Master Di
the Dharma master
(later I went to seek Master Dixian)
, and Master Di said: “These are the seeds of many lives
(these are the karmic seeds from many lives past)
; now, impelled and forced out by the power of the Buddha,
and pressing forward in practice from here, one can pull them out root and stock
(that is, one can root out these karmic seeds)
Master Hanshan, in
A Reply to Commissioner Zheng Kunyan, also has this instruction:

If, when one's practice has reached a point of strength, external conditions no longer enter in, only the afflictions within the mind suddenly rise up all around for no reason whatever. Maybe desires burst forth, maybe the mind grows vexed, maybe all kinds of hindrances arise, so that the mind is weary and the strength spent, and nothing can be done. These are the habitual seeds stored in the alaya-consciousness over countless eons
(also called karmic seeds)

, which today, being pressed hard by the practice, all appear. This is the most critical juncture; one must be clear in his own mind, and first be able to see through it and pass it through, never being overcast by them, never letting them toy with him, never taking them as real matters. Only rouse the spirit, stir up courage and vigor, and
take up the original huatou you are investigating

. If the desires and afflictions still circle and will not leave, then right at the point where these thoughts arise, press after them tightly: I here originally had no such matter — ask whence it came; after all what is it? Resolve to see its settling-place. Pressing it down thus, one only makes ghosts and spirits weep, and they extinguish their traces and hide their tracks. One must certainly drive them to the last and kill them utterly, leaving not a thread behind.
Applying one's strength thus, one naturally sees the good news.

Moreover, when vexation (or weariness, or drowsiness) arises, just observe carefully what kind of feeling it actually is. When you observe it thus, the vexation (or weariness, or drowsiness) gradually becomes less intense and less disturbing, and the mind slowly settles down.
Q: What are the three passes of the Chan gate?
A: The three passes of the Chan gate are: the first pass, the heavy (
chóng

) pass, and the prison pass. The practice of the Chan school is to break these three passes in succession: first, break the first pass (also called breaking the original investigation) to illuminate the mind and see the nature (to see one's original nature through and through); second, break the heavy pass, to cut off afflictions (to sever the delusions of views and thoughts); third, break the prison pass, to realize the patience of no-birth.
